This study introduces a real-time algorithm for detecting events within streams of social media posts. Our approach relies on two key innovations: (1) the introduction of the concept of event "hotspots," and (2) a method that combines spatio-temporal data mining with a Bayesian network to detect events in social media. We have validated our algorithm using Twitter data regarding the 2011 Japan Earthquake and the 2011 London riots. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques, offering significant practical value for event detection. Furthermore, our method is event-agnostic, meaning it does not depend on specific event categories or labels. Finally, we release our code to assist researchers in replicating our methodology. The source code can be accessed at: https://github.com/ChenchenLi1991/Real-time-Spatio-temporal-Event-Detection. Our results indicate that, given the same spatio-temporal distribution, event hotspots tend to emerge earlier in time. Additionally, our approach is more sensitive to events occurring within a specific time window and demonstrates greater robustness to variations in event sizes. The paper's title is: Real-time Spatio-temporal Event Detection on Geotagged Social Media.

High-performance permanent magnets are essential for numerous industrial sectors, including electric vehicles and wind turbines. Yttrium-cobalt-boron magnets are currently utilized in applications requiring both high remanence and high coercivity. While extensive experimental research has focused on optimizing the magnetic properties of yttrium-cobalt-boron compounds by increasing cobalt content, the impact of varying yttrium and boron amounts remains poorly understood. This study employs a high-throughput computational approach to screen cobalt-rich yttrium-cobalt-boron compounds, aiming to identify cobottime-rich materials with enhanced magnetic properties. By combining a high-throughput phase search with magnetic property calculations, we identified 21 cobalt-rich phases. Among these, the YCo$_{19}$B$_{2}$ phase exhibits magnetic moments comparable to Y$_{2}$Co$_{17}$ but demonstrates superior performance. Furthermore, YCo$_{19}$ forms a metastable solid solution with Y$_{2}$Co$_{17}$, potentially enhancing the exchange coupling between phases. These findings offer valuable guidance for the experimental development of high-performance yttrium-cobalt-boron magnets. The dataset, comprising 21 phases with their respective magnetic properties, is accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7210000. It builds upon the widely used Thompson Sampling (TS) method by integrating risk management techniques, specifically Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES), to ensure adaptive budget compliance. Furthermore, the method exhibits robust performance even when dealing with noisy budget usage data. Finally, we outline key directions for future research in this domain. Wigner negativity and quantum steering are two widely used indicators of nonclassicality for continuous-variable quantum states. It is established that all 1-mode Wigner-negative states are steering-positive relative to any mode, yet the converse does not hold. This paper investigates the relationship between these correlations in both bipartite and multi-partite scenarios. We demonstrate that the modes exhibiting steering positive to every Wigner-negative state can be precisely characterized: in the bipartite case, they correspond to Gaussian states, whereas in the multipartite case, they form a convex cone. Additionally, we provide illustrative examples of non-Gaussian states that are steering positive to all Wigner-negative states within both bipartite and multipartite settings. Finally, we explore the connections between these findings and the Robertson-Schrödinger uncertainty relations. These results may facilitate a more profound understanding of the interplay between quantum steering and Wigner negativity. Furthermore, the uncertainty relations derived herein could enable the construction of uncertainty-based inequalities tailored for nonlocal tests involving Wigner-negative states. Notably, this framework may extend to scenarios beyond the continuous-variable domain. Finally, the uncertainty relations established here are expected to find utility in the context of quantum resource theory. Specifically, they can be employed to generate new monotones for quantum coherence, thereby advancing the study of coherence under resource-theoretic principles. Additionally, these relations may serve as valuable tools for designing new quantum protocols. For instance, they can be utilized to enhance the performance of continuous-variable one-way quantum computing models that rely on Wigner-negative states as nonclassical resources. Furthermore, these relations may aid in the design of quantum error-correcting codes, particularly in establishing necessary conditions for the existence of certain codes. Finally, this study may contribute to the development of more efficient and practical methods for generating quantum correlations. Specifically, it may facilitate the design of protocols capable of producing nonlocal correlations without requiring quantum steering as an intermediate resource. In quantum key distribution (QKD) systems employing privacy amplification, the seed random numbers are typically generated by a random number generator (RNG) utilizing entropy from an ambient source. Although modern RNGs are robust, they remain imperfect and may inadvertently allow information leakage to eavesdroppers, creating a security vulnerability. To address this, we propose a security analysis for QKD protocols that accounts for the bounded randomness of the seed. Specifically, we examine the security of schemes utilizing weak measurement and one-way classical post-processing. Our findings indicate that the secure key rate remains unaffected by the bounded nature of the seed when using weak measurement with optimal settings, provided the single-photon source quality is also optimal. Conversely, when either the weak measurement or the single-photon source is suboptimal, the secure key rate is reduced, yet the system can still achieve secure key transmission under certain conditions. These results are derived through universal composability theory, finite-key analysis, and numerical simulations. This study offers a security assessment for QKD systems with privacy amplification under the assumption of imperfect seeds and establishes a foundation for developing secure QKD systems based on ambient entropy. Furthermore, our theoretical framework is applicable to other QKD systems that utilize privacy amplification. This paper establishes that no special timelike Frenet curve counterpart to the well-known classical Bertrand pairs exists. Additionally, we provide the timelike equivalent of the classical mathematical problem that historically drove the development of differential geometry in the 18th and 19th centuries. Finally, we offer a modern solution to the challenge first posed by Euler in the 18th century within the context of semi-Euclidean geometry. The timelike version of this problem is explored here, and we demonstrate that the resulting pair of curves shares the same shape operator, aligning with Euler's original observation in the Euclidean setting. In contrast, when $\theta = 1$, the stationary sampling law corresponds to the density of a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom.

The coalescence distribution for this process is derived by solving the associated backward Feller diffusions equation. The mean time required for two particles starting at distance $x$ to coalesce is calculated as $\frac{\pi}{2\,\kappa}\,\theta$, which diverges to infinity when $\theta = 0$.

$$P_{\text{joint}}(y, t) = e^{-r\,t\,y}\,P_{\text{coal}}(y, t).$$

Boosted Dark Matter offers a promising framework for investigating Dark Matter with mass ranges spanning from the MeV to the TeV scale. In this scenario, Dark Matter particles scatter elastically off atomic nuclei within astrophysical sources, transferring sufficient energy to escape gravitationally and interact with terrestrial detectors. Previous analyses assumed spin-independent interactions; however, this study demonstrates that spin-dependent interactions can significantly enhance sensitivity. Focusing on Dark Matter interacting via the axial vector weak neutral current, we examine sensitivity across astrophysical sources such as the Sun, Galactic Center, and Galactic Cluster Centaurus A. Our findings indicate that the Axion Halo Experiment on the International X-ray Observatory (AXO) could detect Dark Matter with a mass up to 10 GeV through axial photon emission in the Sun, achieving approximately three times greater sensitivity than WIMP searches in coherent neutron scattering. Additionally, we present the first sensitivity projections for AXO through axial gamma-ray emission from the Galactic Center and Centaurus A. We find that AXO can probe effective axial vector couplings as low as $10^{-28} \mathrm{cm}^3$ for Dark Matter masses up to 10 GeV, representing an order of magnitude improvement over current bounds. Furthermore, we show that the search for coherent neutron scattering can probe couplings down to $10^{-29} \mathrm{cm}^3$ for masses up to 100 GeV, surpassing AXO's reach in that mass window. Finally, we demonstrate that axion searches using the Fermi-LAT through the Galactic Center can detect Dark Matter with couplings below $10^{-27} \mathrm{cm}^3$ for masses up to 1 GeV, a sensitivity roughly ten times better than coherent neutron scattering. Notably, the search for boosted Dark Matter in gamma-ray signals from Centaurus A represents a novel avenue for investigating this phenomenon. Conventional non-coherent differential detection for continuous phase modulation (CPM) is recognized for its simplicity and robustness against channel impairments, yet it typically incurs a significant delay relative to the symbol period. This study derives a closed-form expression for the transfer function of the transfer function representation (TFR) of this traditional detector. Leveraging the TFR formulation, the detector structure is enhanced to minimize the delay to nearly one symbol period, achieving this with negligible performance loss. These findings are validated through simulations, and the proposed TFR-based structure is evaluated across various modulation schemes, power spectra, and channel conditions to demonstrate superior delay performance compared to existing detection methods. The TFR formulation and the resulting optimized detector design are applicable to all CPM schemes utilizing constant-amplitude symbols. Furthermore, the research is extended to address frequency-shift keying (FSK) without a phase continuity constraint. The proposed TFR-based delayed detector achieves optimal delay performance for non-coherent detection in this context, reducing the delay to less than one symbol period. Finally, simulation results confirm that this optimized structure outperforms other FSK delayed detectors in terms of delay efficiency. Ultimately, the TFR framework and the associated delayed detector designs represent the most efficient solutions currently available for both traditional and non-phase-continuous non-coherent CPM detection. Additionally, the TFR representation of the traditional detector is shown to be relevant to maximum-likelihood (ML) detection. Keywords: Continuous phase modulation, Delay optimization, Delayed detection, TFR, Non-coherent detection.

Reward learning has recently gained significant attention due to the difficulty of manually designing reward functions for reinforcement learning (RL) agents. However, existing approaches often suffer from either limited scalability or poor sample efficiency. This paper introduces a visually assisted cluster ranking technique that leverages human visual inspection of agent trajectories to identify high-performing actions. By locally clustering similar trajectories, the method facilitates efficient human evaluation, thereby minimizing the number of required samples. Experiments conducted across three benchmark environments in Deep Mind's Control Suite demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art reward learning methods while using 50% fewer samples. This study investigates topological line excitations within frustrated Toric code models, extending the conventional non-frustrated Toric code framework. The model is defined on a three-dimensional cubic lattice where the standard star and plaquette operators are substituted with their frustrated counterparts. By applying duality transformations, a condition for the stability of non-invertible topological line excitations is established. Furthermore, an effective Z₂ topological quantum field theory is constructed to characterize the topological properties of these systems. This TQFT incorporates both topological point and non-topological line excitations, with the latter arising from the condensation of topological point excitations on two-dimensional boundaries. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted on finite lattices to corroborate the theoretical findings. Specifically, the decay of the non-topological line excitation is analyzed by calculating its correlation function, which aligns with theoretical predictions. Additionally, the stability of topological line excitations is demonstrated through the computation of their percolation probability. These results suggest that the proposed frustrated Toric code models serve as a solid foundation for developing topological quantum memory. Finally, the research concludes by discussing the models' potential for error correction and their applicability to quantum computation. Notably, the inclusion of topological line excitations expands the scope of error correction capabilities, while the presence of non-topological line excitations offers a viable pathway for quantum computation. Consequently, these frustrated Toric code models hold significant promise for the advancement of topological quantum technology. We introduce a semantic-driven pre-training approach designed to facilitate dialogue understanding. This method employs an online, unannotated corpus to establish a robust semantic framework for dialogue, thereby eliminating the need for human experts. The corpus is structured into two components: a semantic knowledge base for storing and retrieving information, and a semantic graph that captures the corpus's semantic topology. Specifically, the pre-training process involves extracting semantic information from dialogue utterances and constructing semantic relationships by analyzing interactions between utterances. Consequently, our approach can initiate dialogue understanding tasks—such as slot filling and intent classification—directly from the stored semantic knowledge base, while also supporting the disambiguation of unknown semantic units and the modeling of semantic relationships. Experiments across multiple dialogue datasets, including SN1000, ST1000, ST10000, and SN10K, demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, the approach requires no human annotation and exhibits strong scalability. The source code will be made publicly available.

Algorithmic interpretability is a critical factor in the deployment of machine learning models. While various metrics have been developed to quantify this trait, they often fail to account for algorithm-specific nuances. This paper introduces a framework based on human learning mechanisms to measure algorithmic interpretability, proposing a cognitive complexity score that reflects the difficulty humans face in comprehending algorithms. The effectiveness of this framework is validated through numerical experiments across three algorithm families: decision trees, linear models, and nearest neighbor methods. The results demonstrate that the proposed metric successfully captures the distinct characteristics of algorithmic interpretability. Furthermore, the paper explores potential applications of this measure within machine teaching and algorithm distillation contexts. Finally, the study concludes by identifying limitations of the proposed metric and outlining directions for future research. Unsupervised anomaly detection is a critical task across numerous domains, including security, finance, and healthcare. While deep learning methods have been widely explored, they are often computationally intensive and demand large datasets, limiting their applicability in resource-constrained environments. In contrast, Isolation Forest offers a superior alternative for anomaly detection, delivering high accuracy with reduced complexity. This study introduces TiWS-iForest, a novel approach designed to enhance iForest performance within small datasets (under 100,000 samples) by leveraging weak supervision. The method operates in two phases: first, it expands the dataset through the LADAM algorithm, and second, it further augments it using GANs. The primary objective is to evaluate TiWS-iForest across various benchmark datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in anomaly detection tasks. This paper introduces a new parameterization of the classical Poisson process model designed for light-tailed data, such as rainfall and river discharge. The proposed framework separates the intensity function's scale from its location, offering a distinct advantage: the location parameter exhibits lower sensitivity to the support's upper boundary compared to traditional Pareto-type transformations. This characteristic is particularly valuable for Bayesian extreme value analysis, where posterior inference for location is often a primary objective. The study demonstrates how the new parameterization can be integrated into Bayesian workflows for both stationary and non-stationary threshold-exceedance models. Furthermore, it provides a unified approach for model checking and comparison. A case study on hourly river discharge data from the River Trent at Worksop, UK, illustrates the application of these methods. The paper concludes by discussing the non-stationarity of river flows and forecasting the impacts of climate change. This study theoretically examines the problem of optimizing the average geometric cross-section of a convex body $\mathcal{K}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ under central symmetry, considering an obstacle $\mathcal{D}$ that possesses stationary average cross-sectional values. The analysis employs the average projection body $\mathcal{P}_\pi \mathcal{K}$, defined as the body whose radial function corresponds to the average $(n-1)$-dimensional volume of the projections of $\mathcal{K}$ through the origin. We demonstrate that if the average cross sections of $\mathcal{K}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ coincide at a point $u_0 \in S^{n-1}$, then $u_0$ constitutes a critical point of the function $V(u)$, which represents the volume of $\mathcal{K} \cap u^\perp$. Furthermore, utilizing the average projection body, we establish that if $\mathcal{K}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ share the same average cross section along a $(n-2)$-dimensional subspace, they possess identical average sections for all nearby subspaces, implying that all such subspaces are critical for the volume of $\mathcal{K}$. Additionally, we derive a local optimality result: if the average cross-sectional functions of $\mathcal{K}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ coincide on a $(n-1)$-dimensional subspace, then $\mathcal{K}$ is either an ellipsoid or symmetric with respect to a $(n-2)$-dimensional subspace. Finally, we present a weak Brunn-Minkowski inequality tailored for geometric functionals. These findings generalize and extend various existing results within the field. Notably, the last result serves as a functional analogue to a theorem by F. Morgan and C. Alexander, which states that among all convex bodies with a fixed volume, the ball minimizes the surface area. This implies that balls are critical points for the surface area functional. Our work extends this by identifying all critical points of the surface area functional, revealing that they comprise not only balls but also a broader class of bodies. This significantly expands the understanding of critical points for geometric functionals. Furthermore, our results offer a novel perspective on the derivation of the isoperimetric inequality, as it can be derived from the Minkowski inequality for mixed volumes, which in turn follows from the Alexandrov-Fenchel inequalities. This paper outlines our system for the Commonsense Knowledge (COMET) task, which measures the similarity of word pairs drawn from common sense factography. We evaluated our system at the top rank on all six metrics of COMET-ATOMIC 2020. This study details the approaches and techniques employed, with a primary focus on integrating symbolic commonsense knowledge from large-scale commonsense knowledge graphs (CSKGs) with natural language representations. Specifically, we constructed a word-level representation for the largest CSKGs to date—ConceptNet 15 and ATOMIC 2020—by applying a supervised method to filter out irrelevant words. Additionally, we present a method for retrieving similar word pairs from ATOMIC 2020 to generate candidate knowledge graph factography instances for evaluation. Our research indicates that combining word-level representations derived from CSKGs with neural representations through attention mechanisms yields a system that surpasses state-of-the-art performance. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of COMET-based scoring in downstream tasks, such as word sense disambiguation and natural language inference. Our code and resources are publicly available at https://github.com/robertas-baCOMET. We have conducted a spectroscopic analysis of 10 first-population stars in the globular cluster NGC 2808, utilizing spectra collected with the UVES spectrograph at the ESO-VLT. Our study aims to determine precise and reliable abundance ratios for these stars. Our findings indicate that the stars exhibit a metallicity spread of $\Delta$[Fe/H] = 0.15 dex, with iron abundances ranging from [Fe/H] = -0.81 to -0.66 dex. This spread aligns with recent results from spectroscopic studies of other globular clusters. Additionally, we report significant abundance variations among the light elements, which are consistent with predictions from stellar models incorporating a common origin. The observed variations in Ca, Na, and Al correlate with the [O/Fe] ratio, whereas the behavior of C and N remains ambiguous. These findings suggest that the cluster's first population consists of multiple subpopulations formed through a complex process, likely involving the mixing of material from both the cluster and the galactic halo. Furthermore, the [O/Fe] ratio in NGC 2808 is comparable to that of the solar neighborhood's thin disk, indicating that the cluster's stars may have formed within the disk before being accreted by the Milky Way. Finally, we present the first abundance analysis for the very massive blue straggler BS-1 in NGC 2808, revealing that it shares the same abundance pattern as the cluster's first-population blue stragglers. This supports the hypothesis that BS-1 was formed via binary mass transfer from a main-sequence companion. Single file systems serve as fundamental models for investigating one-dimensional physical systems, with applications spanning from the collective transport of ions through ion channels to the movement of DNA-bound proteins. In this study, we analytically derive the full statistics of the first exit time for a single Brownian particle experiencing strong entropic repulsion as it approaches absorbing boundaries within a two-compartment model. Our derived tailed first exit time distribution reveals that the system's exit time statistics are governed by two distinct time scales, contingent on the particle's initial position. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these dual time scales correspond to two characteristic lengths within the system, which can be understood as superimposed entropic forces. Finally, our theoretical predictions regarding the complete first exit time distribution are validated by numerical simulations. Collectively, these findings offer a comprehensive characterization of the exit time statistics for single file systems. The methodologies employed here can be extended to investigate more complex scenarios, such as ion transport through ion channels. Additionally, the results of this work may find application in single file diffusion processes occurring in various other physical contexts. This study reports initial findings regarding finite volume corrections to the equation of state, trace anomaly, and speed of sound for two specific models: a free, massless scalar theory and quenched QCD utilizing periodic boundary conditions. Additionally, we provide preliminary results for quenched QCD under Dirichlet boundary conditions. Our analysis employs Monte Carlo simulations employing hybrid Monte Carlo algorithms to generate configurations of quasi continuous gluon fields, with non-gluon theories treated as the limit where gluon mass approaches zero. We present the data as functions of both physical volume and dimensionless temperature, defined by the product of temperature and physical volume. In small volumes, we observe significant deviations from the infinite volume equation of state, with differences reaching several tens of percent near the QCD pseudo-critical temperature. These results have direct implications for experiments utilizing heavy ion collisions at very small participant numbers. Furthermore, we discuss the potential for enhancing these calculations through quenched and full QCD. Finally, we address the broader issue of small volume effects in connection with the trace anomaly and speed of sound. Specifically, we demonstrate that using boundary conditions that break Lorentz invariance can result in deviations of up to 50% from infinite volume expectations near the QCD transition temperature. These findings are also highly relevant to experiments involving proton-proton collisions. Our conclusions are supported by the distinct behaviors of the trace anomaly and speed of sound in both small and large volume regimes. Specifically, in small volumes, the trace anomaly exhibits a pronounced peak near the QCD transition region, whereas the speed of sound shows a dip relative to the free gas limit near Lorentz invariant temperatures. In contrast, at large volumes, the trace anomaly displays a broad peak centered on the QCD transition, while the speed of sound rises monotonically from the free gas limit. These latter results are particularly pertinent to the LHC. Finally, we note that the QCD transition in small volumes may not be a universal phenomenon, as it appears to depend on boundary conditions, Lorentz invariance, and potentially other factors. Consequently, the Lorentz invariant speed of sound in small volumes may deviate from the large volume limit, a possibility that could be experimentally testable. We conclude that the small volume QCD transition is likely to be a non-universal phenomenon. The Lyman-alpha (Ly$\alpha$) line at 1216 \AA\ serves as a critical tool for studying the formation and evolution of the first stars and galaxies. However, detecting Ly$\alpha$ emission is difficult because it is typically obscured by neutral hydrogen in the intergalactic medium and the circumgalactic medium. To isolate Ly$\alpha$ photons from the overwhelming continuum background, astronomers employ Lyman filters that block wavelengths both shorter and longer than the line. While current filters for the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope are effective, they are thick and costly. This paper introduces a design for a thin (100 \mu m) and affordable (under \$1000) Lyman filter suitable for ground-based telescopes. The proposed filter utilizes a thin-film interference coating on a polymer membrane, with a prototype version currently under construction. Testing will be conducted at the Gemini Observatory in Chile, where a custom-built optical bench will simulate the specific atmospheric and sky conditions required for ground-based Ly$\alpha$ observations. This study provides a detailed design for the filter and an overview of the prototype's development and testing process. We conclude by discussing the implications of this Lyman filter technology for future astronomical research. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/sguillote/LymanFilter}. Our findings indicate that this prototype can achieve the necessary performance to conduct Ly$\alpha$ photometry. This outcome is supported by the tunability of the filter's transmission curve, the availability of various membrane materials, and the ability to apply these technologies to other spectral lines. Consequently, this work paves the way for utilizing Ly$\alpha$ as a powerful tool for investigating the early universe. The full paper is accessible at \url{https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03001}. This paper introduces a distributed algorithm designed to address two graph symmetric problems: graph cut mean clustering and graph regularized optimal control. Our approach relies on a novel class of distributed graph filters termed "smart filters," which integrate graph Laplacian information into their filter coefficients. These smart filters maintain the property of being positive- and negative-approximate deconvolution filters, a characteristic essential for solving the aforementioned problems in a distributed fashion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed filters operate without explicit knowledge of the global graph structure, thereby enhancing the scalability of the solution. Numerical simulations are provided to validate the efficacy of our method. Additionally, we show that both the clustering and control tasks can be executed concurrently in a distributed manner with reduced communication overhead. Finally, we test the algorithm's performance on real-world data to verify its effectiveness in practical applications. Notably, our proposed clustering method surpasses both traditional and recent state-of-the-art techniques. Active Image Indexing (AII) represents a novel framework for query-by-showing within large image collections. In this paradigm, users indicate a visual target, and the system responds by displaying a set of images that the user can further adjust through additional selections. The system then leverages this interactive feedback to automatically rank the entire database, enabling the user to submit a final submission request. AII is applicable to diverse retrieval tasks, including similarity, next-image prediction, and augmented reality, and is particularly valuable when users can provide complex, multimodal, or domain-specific constraints. We present a flexible architecture for building various AII systems using modern deep neural networks and user interaction capabilities. To evaluate our approach, we developed a new benchmark task: query-by-showing virtual-to-real augmented reality search. This task requires searching through extensive video and image datasets to locate 3D objects captured in real-world videos, where users can provide both 2D and 3D feedback. Our top-performing AII system achieved a success rate of 60% on the 100-object DeepFashionAR+ dataset, outperforming the next best method by a significant margin. The complete system is available at https://github.com/robertkember/active-image-indexing. The source code for the next-image and 3d-search tasks will be released upon acceptance. This work demonstrates the versatility of AII and establishes a new benchmark for interactive query-by-showing in large image collections. The proposed framework is compatible with various tasks, domains, and modalities, and is built upon cutting-edge deep neural networks. Our results set new state-of-the-art records across all evaluated tasks. Furthermore, the integration of user feedback and active learning sets a new standard for query-by-showing retrieval, while the evaluation on 3D search tasks introduces a new dimension to the field. Finally, the emphasis on interactive and active approaches marks a significant shift in how large image collections are searched and utilized. This study investigates keyless authentication for independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sources over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels, where the receiver generates an anonymous claim about the sender's message that the verifier must verify. We examine the performance of a new, straightforward scheme utilizing source statistics and compare it against an existing approach by Li and Alpcan [IEEE Trans. Inf. Forensics Security 14, 2019], which relies on artificial noise. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that the keyless scheme outperforms the artificial noise method when sufficient source statistics are available at the receiver. Furthermore, numerical evaluations confirm that this advantage grows with the level of source statistics. Finally, we establish that the keyless framework is strictly superior to artificial noise even in the limiting case of very rare messages. In this regime, we derive closed-form expressions for the sender and verifier success probabilities, as well as the probability of a successful spoofing attack. These results indicate that with adequate source statistics, the sender and verifier achieve near-certain success, while verifier spoofing attacks are suppressed to near zero. Conversely, when source statistics are scarce, success rates remain high for both legitimate parties and adversaries. Additionally, we characterize the optimal keyless scheme by solving a convex optimization problem. This optimality is particularly pronounced for rare messages and high source statistics. However, even under these favorable conditions, we observe a non-negligible attack success probability, suggesting that keyless authentication may be infeasible for highly rare messages despite ample source statistics. We anticipate that these findings will be valuable for researchers developing authentication schemes for resource-constrained devices. Finally, we discuss potential extensions of this work to other source models and channel types. Specifically, for Gaussian sources, we show that source compression can enhance keyless authentication performance. Regarding channels, we extend the analysis to discrete memoryless channels (DMCs) and provide a characterization of the optimal keyless scheme for a specific class of DMCs. Although the current analysis is limited to Gaussian sources and specific channel models, we believe it will serve as a foundation for future research into keyless authentication across broader source and channel domains. Ultimately, we aim to advance the field of keyless authentication as a practical solution for resource-limited devices. We demonstrate that while the exact solution to the Schrödinger equation for a particle with initial momentum $\kappa_0$ traveling down a tilted potential washboard exhibits dispersionless behavior at early times, it undergoes significant spreading at later times. In contrast, a wave packet with a narrow initial width maintains low spreading, ensuring that the diffusion coefficient remains finite. Furthermore, we establish that the Hegerfeldt paradox does not impede particle flow in this scenario. Finally, we analyze the impact of dephasing, showing that it induces a peak in the diffusion coefficient at finite winding numbers. These findings are illustrated using the Anderson model. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the winding number and the winding number density for both real and complex times. Our results indicate that, within the narrow-width approximation, the winding number density approaches that of a free particle, whereas in the dephasing regime, it displays oscillatory patterns. Additionally, we observe that the winding number density for a real initial state is higher than that of a dephased state. Finally, the study investigates the probability density distribution of winding numbers, revealing that for a real initial state, the distribution is symmetric around zero, whereas for a dephased state, it becomes asymmetric. This asymmetry is characterized by a longer tail extending into positive winding numbers for winding numbers less than one, and into negative winding numbers for winding numbers greater than one. We attribute this asymmetry to the interplay between dephasing and the winding number density. These findings are demonstrated using the generalized Aubry-Andr\'e model. Finally, we explore the connection between winding numbers and rare events. Specifically, we show that the probability density distribution of winding numbers for a real initial state follows a Gaussian distribution, whereas for a dephased state, it adheres to a power-law distribution. This distinction arises from the differing behaviors of the winding number density in the dephased and undephasied regimes. This paper presents a flexible local projection method designed to estimate impulse responses to various shocks. The approach constructs nonparametric estimates of conditional expectation functions for projected output variables, utilizing observations up to a specific horizon $H$ post-shock. The estimator's flexibility allows researchers to adapt it to the data characteristics of different response coefficients. The study derives asymptotic normality for the estimator at any horizon within $H$ and develops a bootstrap procedure to estimate the conditional covariance matrix. Empirical analysis applies these tools to assess the sensitivity of impulse responses to identification methods and the selection of the cutoff horizon $H$. Furthermore, the paper examines the identification of impulse responses when $H$ extends to infinity. Applications cover estimated responses to monetary policy shocks, a structural vector autoregression with a rich set of controls, and survey data on unexpected news regarding monetary policy. Additionally, a software package implementing this estimator is made available. Online supplementary material includes further applications on identification sensitivity, the performance of inference and estimation in finite samples, and additional examples. Finally, another section of supplementary material provides details on the asymptotic theory and simulation experiments. The associated software package offers the estimation and bootstrap procedures, along with code for all online supplementary material examples. We examine the angular momentum of a charge $q$ rotating within a uniform magnetic field, investigating the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum. The orbital angular momentum of the charge, known as the Casimir momentum, scales with $\hbar c/\mathcal{B}$ and is shared equally between the two magnetic sublevels of the Landau levels. In contrast, our spin-orbit analysis demonstrates that the spin-orbit term cancels out, leaving only this angular Casimir momentum. Furthermore, we calculate the torque exerted on a dipole representing the charge's angular momentum, revealing its dependence on time, light speed, and the magnetic field, while notably being independent of the reduced Planck constant. Finally, as an application, we compute the rate at which this vacuum torque extracts energy from a nonrelativistic charge undergoing uniform circular motion in the magnetic field. This torque opposes the motion, and the resulting power loss scales with $\mathcal{B}$. This finding contrasts with the case of a spin-orbit term, where power loss would be independent of $\mathcal{B}$. Consequently, the magnetic field can be tuned to control vacuum-induced vacuum stirring, spin-orbit coupling, and power loss. These results align with those of a rotating dipole, underscoring the validity of the analogy between the angular Casimir momentum of a Landau charge and an Einstein dipole. Our findings may also have implications for the Einstein-Maxwell equations, black hole angular momentum, and the no-hair theorem. Additionally, the classical power loss associated with this angular Casimir momentum can be interpreted as a magnetic drag force, which may be relevant to the quantum friction experienced by a magnetically rotating neutral particle. Finally, the vacuum torque acting on the charge's angular momentum may contribute to the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of a black hole. Overall, the vacuum torque, spin-orbit coupling, and the classical and quantum analogies between an Einstein dipole and a Landau charge suggest that the quantum vacuum stirs when a charge rotates. This stirring effect is particularly pronounced in superconductors, where Landau levels are quantized due to the presence of a magnetic field. Furthermore, the quantum vacuum's response to a Landau charge may offer a solution to the Unruh effect. Specifically, an accelerating superconducting charge could induce a response in the quantum vacuum, potentially explaining the temperature experienced by an observer. Game theory offers a framework for analyzing interactions between self-interested agents, with Nash equilibrium serving as the primary solution concept. Although valuable, Nash equilibria are frequently difficult to compute and can be ambiguous since multiple equilibria may exist. To address this computational challenge, we introduce rationalization value prediction, a new machine learning task designed to estimate whether a game's true rationalizable values include a specific value. We demonstrate that rationalizable set prediction is both distinct from and more demanding than standard value prediction. To address the prediction of Nash equilibria, we propose NashRationalizableFPNets, a method that leverages rationalization to enhance accuracy. Our evaluation utilizes synthetic games, as well as real-world applications from supply and demand, portfolio selection, and traffic routing. These findings indicate that rationalization set prediction is a novel and critical task for predicting rational agent behavior, and that our approach effectively improves the prediction of both rationalizable and Nash equilibria. Furthermore, we observe that agents are often rationalizable even when their payoffs are not strictly rational, suggesting that rationalizability better captures the complexity of human decision-making. Finally, we show that FPNets can be adapted to compute rationalizable sets, offering a promising pathway for developing new rationalizable solution concepts. This work opens avenues for further research into the rationalizability of human choices. Code is available at https://github.com/ashwinb22/rationalizable_set_prediction.

This study addresses the challenge of bounding causal effects when treatment assignment is dependent on unobserved variables. Building on the framework introduced by Shpitser and Tian (2007), we introduce dimensionality reduction techniques for these bounds, thereby expanding their applicability. We evaluate the performance of these derived bounds using simulated data. The findings indicate that the bounds offer tight constraints on causal effects in high-dimensional contexts, though they may be overly conservative in low-dimensional settings. Additionally, we explore methods for enhancing these bounds by leveraging knowledge of treatment effect sparsity. Our results demonstrate that the confidence intervals generated by these sparsity-based bounds are significantly narrower than those produced by the original approach of Shpitser and Tian (2007). Finally, we apply these sparsity-informed bounds to real-world data to assess the impact of Medicaid expansion on labor supply within the context of the Health and Retirement Study. This work introduces a method for monitoring linear time-invariant systems against stealthy attacks, ensuring that system outputs remain within linear constraints. The proposed algorithm utilizes a Kalman filter to generate state estimates, which are then projected onto the constraint set. This approach is computationally efficient, avoiding the need for online convex optimization. The paper provides an analysis of the method's performance regarding constraint violation probabilities and establishes a corresponding bound on the average violation count. Furthermore, the relationship between these violation metrics and the system's minimum detectable attack direction is explored. Finally, the algorithm is validated through a numerical case study. The results demonstrate that the method achieves a significant reduction in constraint violations with only a marginal increase in computational cost. Additionally, the study confirms that the derived theoretical bounds on average constraint violations are tight. Autonomous document summarization has garnered significant attention due to its extensive applications. This work defines S-rings of Krull type and outlines their fundamental properties and characterizations. Furthermore, for an S-ring $S$ of Krull type, we identify the maximal $S$-ideals and provide the factorization of the quotient $S/S_\mathfrak{p}$ for any prime $S_\mathfrak{p}$ that is not maximal. Additionally, we derive a formula for the quotient fields of $S$ and establish criteria for the existence of quasi-free $S$-rings of Krull type with a finite number of quotient fields. Finally, we investigate the properties of S-rings of Krull type formed by the integral closure of regular $S$-rings of finite type within their quotient fields. In this context, we demonstrate the existence of free S-rings of Krull type, provide factorizations for their prime ideals, and determine their free ring bases. Furthermore, we construct a canonical factorization for prime ideals in these S-rings of Krull type and develop a criterion for their separability. The study is supported by 15 references. **Aims.** The presence of companions, including planets, significantly influences the rotation periods and chemical abundances of their host stars. This study seeks to constrain the masses and separations of potential companions for five accelerating stars by analyzing their photometric light curves. **Methods.** We conducted a thorough search for periodic signals in the light curves of these five stars, which were previously identified as accelerating. **Results.** We identified a 10.6-day period in the light curve of HD 101065, indicating a small companion with a mass of approximately 0.001 M$_{\odot}$. Additionally, we detected a 1.5-year period in HD 101095, suggesting the presence of a small companion at a separation of roughly 1.5 AU. For HD 101096, the lack of periodicity in the light curve allows us to rule out companions with masses between 0.001 and 0.01 M$_{\odot}$ at separations of 0.5 to 1.5 AU. **Conclusions.** This work demonstrates that the light curves of accelerating stars can be utilized to detect small, close companions. The findings will aid in understanding the impact of companions on stellar properties and evolution. Furthermore, the results for HD 101065 and HD 101095 are consistent with the hypothesis that the observed orbital motion of their companions caused the measured stellar acceleration. Finally, the results for HD 101096 are also compatible with the hypothesis that acceleration due to orbital motion explains the observed stellar acceleration. Overall, the light curves of these five stars do not show evidence of large companions. **Keywords.** planetary systems: masses and evolutions; planetary systems: separations; planetary systems: detection; planetary systems: statistics; planetary systems: individual: HD 101065; planetary systems: individual: HD 101095; planetary systems: individual: HD 101096; planetary systems: individual: HD 101098; planetary systems: individual: HD 101099. **Abbreviation.** MESA: Modules for Experiments in Stellar Astrophysics. **Acknowledgements.** This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) under grant 11773031. The autoencoder serves as a potent unsupervised technique for feature extraction and dimensionality reduction. In this study, we introduce a regularized Variational Bayesian (VB) autoencoder, where the encoder is formulated as a Bayesian model and the autoencoder is trained using a least squares objective. Our objective is to mitigate overfitting during training by applying an $\ell_1$ penalty to the learned weights. This approach yields a sparse autoencoder that effectively eliminates redundant features. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses the performance of both the standard VB autoencoder and the sparse autoencoder. Extensive experiments conducted on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets underscore the superiority of our method. The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has significantly increased security and privacy concerns within smart home environments. This paper introduces a low-cost, secure framework designed to securely manage numerous IoT devices in residential settings. The proposed solution for smart home security and data privacy leverages blockchain and RSSI-based trilateration for localization. Blockchain offers security, immutability, and data integrity, while the localization mechanism facilitates data sharing among authorized users. Additionally, blockchain supports data monetization, enabling homeowners to sell their data to third parties. This combination of blockchain and localization not only enhances security but also improves energy efficiency. We have developed a prototype of this framework and conducted experimental studies to validate the proposed approach. The results demonstrate that the method is both efficient and effective. The study includes an evaluation of the blockchain network's performance regarding throughput and transaction latency. Furthermore, the accuracy of the localization algorithm was tested under varying transmission power levels and different numbers of anchor nodes. Ultimately, the proposed framework is shown to be efficient, effective, and cost-efficient. A comprehensive comparison of the blockchain-based smart home security framework against existing approaches is provided in the conclusion. The findings indicate that this framework is superior to current solutions in terms of throughput, transaction latency, and energy efficiency. Consequently, the blockchain-based approach is proven to be more secure and energy-efficient than traditional methods. The paper concludes by discussing potential future extensions of this proposed framework. Through blockchain technology, smart homes can achieve greater security, data privacy, and energy efficiency. Ultimately, this blockchain-based solution is expected to play a critical role in the future development of smart homes. Keywords: Blockchain, IoT, Smart Home, Security, Privacy, Localization, RSSI.

This paper introduces a deep learning-based approach to quantify Lloyd-Eliasmith-Lee (L-LV) values for gray-coded modulation schemes. The core concept involves training a deep neural network (DNN) to perform the L-LV quantization of an L-LV angle. To facilitate this, an L-LV angle is defined as a rotation applied to a L-LV cube within an L-LV modulation scheme, which is a hypercube formed by arranging L-LV constellation points. This angle is generated by a deep neural network designed to maximize the mutual information between the angle and the constellation. The proposed DNN is trained to optimize the performance of a digital communication system utilizing L-LV modulation. The paper provides a detailed description of the DNN architecture and training methodology, followed by a simulation study comparing the proposed scheme against a random L-LV angle approach. Results indicate that the proposed method achieves a 20% reduction in the number of bits required to describe the L-LV constellation. Furthermore, simulations demonstrate that the proposed scheme outperforms the random angle approach in both QAM and non-QAM contexts. Finally, the study explores the application of L-LV modulation in optical communication systems. Numerical simulations reveal that the proposed scheme surpasses existing L-LV schemes in both QAM and non-QAM scenarios. Additionally, the results show that the proposed scheme can exceed the performance of standard QAM in QAM cases and the performance of existing non-QAM schemes in non-QAM cases. The paper concludes that the proposed scheme is effective for both QAM and non-QAM applications. Keywords: L-LV Modulation, Deep Learning, DNN, Optical Communication, QAM, Non-QAM.

This study examines the classical problem of determining if a directed acyclic graph (DAG) can be embedded in the plane such that all edges follow a specific coordinate axis. While Upward Planarity Testing is solvable in linear time for 1-planar DAGs, it remains NP-complete for 2-planar DAGs, with no known parameterized algorithms for intermediate cases. We introduce a parameterized algorithm for 3-planar DAGs that achieves a running time of $O(3^{p^2} \cdot \text{poly}(n))$, where $p$ denotes the planarity deficiency and $n$ is the number of vertices. Furthermore, we present a parameterized algorithm for genus planar DAGs with a complexity of $O(2^{p^3} \cdot \text{poly}(n))$. Our methodology relies on a novel technique for identifying UV-minors, which we demonstrate to be of independent interest and potential application in broader contexts. Finally, we propose a conjecture suggesting that genus planar DAGs admit a parameterized algorithm with a running time of $O(2^{p^2} \cdot \text{poly}(n))$. We validate this conjecture for Euler planar DAGs by providing an algorithm with the desired complexity of $O(2^{p^2}n^3)$. Notably, this result surpasses the best previously known algorithm for the Upward Planarity Testing problem. Additionally, we establish that the problem is NP-hard when $p$ is treated as an input rather than a parameter. Our findings are based on a preprint available at arXiv:2101.01001. Finally, the source code for the algorithm can be accessed at https://github.com/ashwinb/UV-Minors. Our implementation successfully handles instances with up to 1000 vertices and a planarity deficiency of 30. We anticipate that our research will inspire further advancements in the field of upward planarity. This study addresses the challenge of analyzing datasets contaminated with noise, a common issue in crowdsourced data where human annotators may assign incorrect labels. We examine the impact of noise on both hard-label and soft-label datasets, introducing a novel ensemble method that surpasses state-of-the-art ensemble models on small-scale noisy datasets. Additionally, we propose a new uncertainty metric called "Human Softmax," which quantifies uncertainty derived from the distribution of annotator labels. This new measure is evaluated against two existing uncertainty techniques. Finally, our methodology is benchmarked against three leading uncertainty measures found in the literature. Our results demonstrate that the proposed ensemble strategy, which leverages the complementary strengths of various uncertainty measures, yields superior performance compared to existing approaches. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/alextucker1994/ensemble-methods. This work is based on the research paper titled: "An Approach Noisy, Crowdsourced Datasets Utilizing Ensemble Modeling, 'Human Softmax' Distributions, and Entropic Measures of Uncertainty."

We demonstrate exponential decay in the Hölder norm for transfer operators acting on smooth observables within uniformly and nonuniformly expanding semiflows that exhibit exponential decay of correlations. This approach extends the results of Pollicott and Ruelle (1986), who originally established these decay rates for flows on hyperbolic manifolds, to encompass a broader range of scenarios. Additionally, our proof offers a self-contained and streamlined alternative to the arguments previously presented by Burq and Koch (2006). Finally, we illustrate an application of these findings to the analysis of local statistics. Specifically, we investigate the distribution of return times to small targets for nonuniformly expanding semiflows, a problem that generalizes the study of Pugh and Sullivan (1987) regarding geodesic flows on negatively curved manifolds. We demonstrate that the scaling required to obtain nontrivial limits is optimal and that the limiting distribution is unique. Furthermore, the methodology employed is more direct and more general than the recent work by Climenhaga and Pesin (2019). Our findings also extend to infinite-dimensional settings, including infinite-dimensional Axiom A attractors and smooth hyperbolic parabolic equations. The initial section of the paper is specifically dedicated to addressing the more challenging case of nonuniformly expanding semiflows. Our strategy involves utilizing the contact structure inherent in the semiflow to reduce the transfer operator for the semiflow to the product of transfer operators defined on the Poincaré map and the base semiflow. This technique relies on a recent advancement by the authors and applies to any smooth contact semiflow. We demonstrate that this approach is sufficiently robust to handle contact semiflows with nontrivial recurrence, a phenomenon that precludes the construction of a local section near the periodic orbit. Our findings are also applicable to infinite-dimensional semiflows, such as smooth hyperbolic parabolic equations and infinite-dimensional Axiom A attractors. The paper begins with an application to the Burgers equation, followed by a discussion of semiflows on infinite-dimensional spaces. In this context, we extend the results of Mañé (1983) concerning the statistical behavior of periodic orbits on hyperbolic invariant manifolds. Our results also apply to semiflows that are not analytic, provided they satisfy a specific condition on the Lie derivative of the contact form. We also examine the statistical properties of periodic orbits for the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation, a scenario where the contact structure is absent.

A strength $t$ covering array, denoted as $\text{CA}(N;t,k,q)$, is an $N \times k$ matrix utilizing symbols from a set of size $q$, where every possible $t$-tuple appears in at least one $t \times k$ subarray. The order $N$ is defined as the covering array size. When every $t$-tuple appears in at least $\lambda$ subarrays, it is termed a $\lambda$-covering array. This study focuses on covering arrays with small parameters, specifically where $t=2$ and $q=3$. By integrating computational searches with theoretical analysis, we characterize the structure of minimal strength $2$ covering arrays under these constraints. Leveraging the fact that strength $2$ covering arrays over GF$(q)$ correspond to arc-colored graphs, we utilize algebraic graph theory to construct examples with near-optimal parameters. This characterization enables the determination of the exact covering array size $\text{CA}(N;2,3,3)$ for $4 \leq N \leq 14$, resolving an open problem posed by Colbourn and Leavitt in 1992. Furthermore, we provide the complete distribution of nonisomorphic arrays for these values. Our findings demonstrate that the size of the smallest covering array for $q=3, t=2, k=4$ is $9$, improving upon the previous best lower bound of $10$. Additionally, we present the covering array spectrum for $q \leq 6$, identifying the minimum sizes across various parameter sets. For $q=3$, we offer the first comprehensive characterization of the distribution of covering arrays given fixed $N$ and $k$. The resulting arrays serve as valuable test cases for constraint satisfaction solvers. Finally, we characterize the smallest $\lambda$-covering arrays for $q=3, t=2$ where $1 \leq \lambda \leq 5$. The existence of an intermediate square-square vortex lattice phase within a two-dimensional high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate superconductor has been demonstrated through vortex correlation analysis of scanning tunneling microscope data from Bi$_2$Se$_{1-x}$S$_x$SeCuo$_4$. This specific phase emerges in underdoped samples where the superconducting critical temperature $T_\textrm{c}$ is significantly below the pseudogap temperature $T^*$, a condition that amplifies vortex-lattice anisotropy. The ability to identify this phase in an experimentally accessible high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate suggests that similar transition phases may exist across a broader range of high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate families. Furthermore, the discovery of this phase offers a potential explanation for the anomalous specific heat behavior observed in underdoped Bi$_2$Se$_{1-x}$S$_x$SeCuo$_4$. Finally, the presence of this phase in a high-$T_\textrm{c}$ cuprate supports the hypothesis that pseudogap physics is intrinsically linked to vortex-lattice anisotropy. These findings provide compelling evidence for a phase that was previously identified only through theoretical predictions and numerical simulations. Photons emitted from a viscous quark-gluon plasma (QGP) generated in heavy-ion collisions exhibit anisotropic flow, with their slope providing critical insights into the plasma's properties. We utilized thermal photon spectra from the ALICE experiment at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 2.76$ TeV to constrain the QGP's shear viscosity. Our thermal photon model incorporates both viscous and thermal corrections derived from the Boltzmann equation, alongside a reanalysis of the horizon scan results by Caron-Huot et al. [1405.7024] to determine the thermal component. By integrating viscous and thermal corrections with viscous hydrodynamic model results, we calculated thermal photon spectra and compared them against ALICE experimental data. Our findings indicate that the thermal component of thermal photons is highly sensitive to QGP shear viscosity, with the photon spectral slope offering the most stringent constraints on this parameter. Consequently, the spectral slope can serve as an effective metric for the QGP's shear viscosity. Furthermore, we computed the shear viscosity-to-overlapping density ratio, $\eta/s$, for the QGP using the temperature-dependent interaction cross section $\sigma_{\rm int}$ between light and heavy quarks within the lattice QCD framework of Liu et al. [1005.3039]. Our results demonstrate that $\eta/s$ is a temperature-dependent quantity, a conclusion that aligns with lattice QCD calculations. Finally, we observed that the spectral slope is more pronounced at lower transverse momenta, $p_{\rm T}$. This work establishes a foundation for future research aimed at extracting the QGP's shear viscosity from thermal photon spectra. **Keywords:** thermal photon, shear viscosity, thermal photon spectral slope, $\eta/s$, lattice QCD. **PACS numbers:** 25.75.-q, 25.75.-q, 25.75.Lk, 12.38.Gc, 12.38.Aw. **PACS:** 25.75.-q, 25.75.-q, 25.75.Lk, 12.38.Gc, 12.38.Aw. **arXiv eprint:** 1405.7024. **PACS:** 25.75.-q, 25.75.-q, 25

We introduce a novel statistical framework for identifying causal effects within large-scale, high-throughput experiments characterized by a vast number of primary outcomes. This approach addresses scenarios where causal estimates are correlated and certain outcomes may lack sufficient variation to estimate these effects. Our method integrates two recent advancements: the adaptation of minP tests to handle zero-variance units and the application of thresholding to eliminate unit-level causal estimates that fall below a specified magnitude. This strategy allows for controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) among units that actually exhibit a non-zero treatment effect, even in the presence of complex dependencies. To implement this procedure, we propose a data-splitting design that separates units into subsets for FDR threshold estimation and for calculating the distribution of test statistics. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness through both a simulation study and an analysis of a large-scale genomic experiment. Furthermore, our approach is designed to remain robust against violations resulting from the separation of units into different subsets. Finally, we have made the method accessible via an R package. *Keywords:* Causal inference, false discovery rate, high-dimensional data, minP test, treatment effect detection, genomic screens. *Software:* *Tefos*. The fundamental concepts of cosmological inflation are examined. We derive the equations of motion governing the inflaton field, define the slow-roll parameters, and outline the calculation of inflationary perturbations along with their relationship to the temperature anisotropies observed in the cosmic microwave background. Furthermore, the basic principles of reheating following the inflationary epoch are addressed. As an illustrative case, the dynamics of slow-roll inflation driven by a quadratic inflaton potential are derived, and the slow-roll approximation is tested against this specific model. We also compute the power spectrum and temporal correlation function for perturbations in a quadratic potential, subsequently analyzing the resulting cosmic microwave background anisotropies. The discussion concludes with a brief overview of two additional inflaton potential types: the Hilltop potential and Natural Inflation. Finally, we highlight the main shortcomings of the inflationary framework and suggest potential future developments. This account is intentionally non-exhaustive, intentionally omitting detailed treatments of the expansion of the universe's horizon during inflation, the generation of primordial gravitational waves, the framework for calculating the Lyman-$\alpha$ power spectrum, the theory of structure formation, and the integration of inflation with quantum gravity. These topics will be addressed in forthcoming papers. The objective is to provide a clear summary of current understanding while offering insights into plausible future directions. Wherever possible, all statements are supported by references to the literature. The material is designed to be accessible to graduate students and early-career researchers, though some sections may require advanced background. Nevertheless, an attempt has been made to ensure logical flow and clarity. Given the extensive scope, errors are inevitable; however, it is hoped that the discussion remains rigorous. This text serves as a supplement to the book series *Lectures in Physics*, Volume 62, published by Springer-Verlag, Berlin, Germany, 2014. Comments are welcome at email: email@example.com.

The CDF II collaboration has recently reported a precise measurement of the $W$ boson mass that deviates from the Standard Model prediction by approximately $7\sigma$. This observed shift suggests a non-Standard Model contribution to the $W$ mass at the few-per-mille level. A Type-X two Higgs doublet model (2HDM) can account for this deviation, provided the Higgs boson coupling to muons is roughly $300$ times that of electrons. However, this large coupling renders the muon $g-2$ highly sensitive to the Type-X 2HDM. Given the existing tension between the $W$ mass anomaly and the muon $g-2$ measurement, we examine the compatibility of both within this framework. Our findings indicate that a common explanation for the $W$ mass and muon $g-2$ requires fine-tuning of the Type-X 2HDM parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the $g\bar{g}\phi$ coupling is significantly enhanced compared to other scenarios, offering a potential solution to the $125$ GeV Higgs excess observed at the LHC. Finally, we show that various experimental measurements can distinguish the Type-X 2HDM from the Standard Model. Notably, we find that the charged Higgs mass limit derived from the $B\to X_{s}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ decay is compatible with the $W$ mass anomaly but excludes the muon $g-2$ contribution. In contrast, the future high-luminosity LHC will be able to probe the muon $g-2$ contribution through the $B\to D^{(*)}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ decay. Additionally, we show that the $\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$-fused Higgs boson production at a muon collider can test the large muon Yukawa coupling in the Type-X 2HDM. Finally, we demonstrate that the $\mu^{+}\mu^{-}\to HAA$ process at a muon collider can provide evidence for the second Higgs doublet in the Type-X 2HDM. Software developers frequently encounter queries regarding the location of concepts, a scenario that has driven extensive research into effective query reformulation strategies. This paper introduces QUICKAR, a method that automatically reformulates queries for concept location by leveraging crowdsourced knowledge. The approach employs a novel, straightforward technique to generate reformulations, subsequently ranking them to identify the most probable target concept. We conducted an empirical study to evaluate QUICKAR's effectiveness in improving concept localization. The results indicate that the proposed method successfully generates a high volume of high-quality queries. Furthermore, QUICKAR surpassed existing query reformulation techniques in both precision and recall. Our findings confirm that this automatic reformulation approach significantly enhances the utility of concept locators. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12/QUICKAR. Entrainment is a recognized social-communicative mechanism where individuals subtly mimic specific utterance features to foster rapport. This study introduces an unsupervised deep neural network approach to calculate the distance between two such features, yielding a distance metric that offers a promising framework for future research. Specifically, we investigate acoustic, prosodic, and semantic features, finding that the distance matrix for spectral features most effectively captures various aspects of entrainment. Furthermore, we empirically demonstrate that this proposed distance metric significantly outperforms several existing alternatives. Finally, we illustrate that the method can empirically validate key properties of entrainment, such as reciprocity and symmetry, in conversational data. Additionally, the distance matrix for spectral features proves effective for visualizing entrainment patterns through a newly developed visualization technique. Overall, this unsupervised approach to quantifying entrainment is expected to advance future research in this field. Temporal action segmentation is a critical task for learning-based systems, yet it demands substantial labeled data. To address the scarcity of annotations, we introduce SSCAP, an approach that performs temporal action segmentation without relying on any labeled information. SSCAP is grounded in the insight that actions within a video frequently co-occur, a pattern that is consistent across different datasets. Our method is fully unsupervised, utilizing self-supervised learning for both feature extraction and action labeling. Specifically, we develop an unsupervised contrastive learning technique to generate dataset-agnostic features capable of distinguishing various action categories. For temporal action segmentation, we propose an action representation model based on action-action co-occurrence, which is trained without annotated data. This model represents actions as the probability of an action's occurrence given the presence of other actions. We validate SSCAP's efficacy through benchmark comparisons on two datasets, showing that it achieves competitive performance in temporal action segmentation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that SSCAP can be applied to annotate videos with temporal action labels, which we empirically show to be effective for supervised action recognition. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets confirm the effectiveness and robustness of our method. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/Chenchen2020/SSCAP. Using the framework of current algebra, we investigate the many-body currents responsible for the formation of pentaquark states and their subsequent decay into baryon-meson pairs. This approach incorporates both the explicit charm quark content of the pentaquarks and their decay products, as well as the sea-charm component within many-body currents that facilitates the creation of charmed pairs. We calculate the production cross sections for $\Lambda_c$ and $\Sigma_c$ pentaquarks in the reaction $\gamma p \to P_{_{\rm I, II}} (\to \Sigma_c N) \pi$, identifying two distinct contributions: one driven by the explicit charm in the Fierz rearrangement of the vertex, and another arising from sea-charm in the diagrammatic calculation. For the decay processes $P_{_{\rm I, II}} \to \Sigma_c N \pi$, we derive the decay widths by evaluating the relevant hadronic transition amplitudes. Furthermore, we provide numerical estimates for the production cross sections and relevant decay branching ratios. Our findings indicate that the production of $P_{_{\rm I, II}}$ states via the explicit charm mechanism is highly suppressed, whereas the sea-charm contribution is substantial. Additionally, our predicted decay widths for $P_{_{\rm I, II}}$ align well with experimental measurements. Consequently, our results suggest that both production and decay of pentaquark states are significantly influenced by sea-charm, thereby offering a deeper understanding of their internal structures. This underscores the necessity of conducting both production and decay studies of pentaquarks at high-luminosity facilities such as the Electron-Ion Collider. Finally, we offer several perspectives on future research directions. Specifically, we propose that the production cross sections for $P_{_{\rm I, II}}$ at the Electron-Ion Collider could be large enough to enable precise measurements of their spin-parity quantum numbers.
