In the classic stable marriage problem, individuals rank potential partners, and a stable marriage is one where no two individuals prefer each other over their current partners. The well-known Gale-Shapley algorithm generates a unique solution by having one group of individuals, such as men, sequentially propose to their preferred choices until all are matched. This algorithm guarantees a solution but overlooks individual preferences regarding specific proposals. We introduce a generalized solution where individuals can selectively choose which proposals to make, provided they value their current match more than any new opportunity. This broader framework is more flexible and can model various decision-making scenarios. Furthermore, we establish conditions ensuring individual existence and solvability, and we examine the existence of individual regret, defined as receiving a match worse than a chosen proposal. Finally, we analyze individual existence, solvability, and regret for both the marriage problem and its many-sided extension. Specifically for the many-sided version, we identify conditions under which a solution exists and can be found, where individuals are paired into groups rather than one-on-one, and individual regret is minimized. These findings are particularly relevant to real-world applications like the National Resident Matching Program. Our results demonstrate that when individuals can select which proposals to make, regret is significantly reduced, and the time required to find a solution decreases substantially. Additionally, we present a numerical study comparing our proposed solution method with existing algorithms. The study indicates that our approach requires less time to compute a solution compared to current methods. Keywords: Stable matching, stable marriage, many-sided stable matching, individual regret, individual existence, solvability. Mathematics Subject Classification: 05C60, 91B06, 91B12, 91B26.

Summary generation models are typically assessed using generation-based techniques like ROUGE, which measure similarity to ideal summaries. However, these methods fail to assess semantic equivalence, leading to debates about their reliability. To address this, sequence-to-sequence encoders have been introduced to calculate similarity against reference summaries. Building on these approaches, we present SummScore, a comprehensive evaluation metric designed to gauge the semantic quality of generated summaries. SummScore employs a cross-encoder architecture to compute an overall quality score. It calculates three distinct scores—relevance, coherence, and factuality—by comparing model outputs against both human and machine-generated reference summaries. Furthermore, SummScore supports multi-document scenarios, allowing for the evaluation of summaries against other summaries rather than just reference texts. Extensive experiments across various models and datasets demonstrate that SummScore yields more informative and interpretable scores than existing metrics. Additionally, SummScore exhibits strong correlation with human annotations, indicating its effectiveness in accurately measuring summary quality. This work introduces a rapid algorithm for reconstructing sparse signals from quadratic measurements. We first present a convex optimization framework that guarantees accurate recovery with high probability. Subsequently, we develop a non-convex approach with guaranteed convergence to a point that satisfies the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions of the convex problem, enabling its efficient implementation. LiDAR's resilience to illumination changes and motion blur makes it an ideal companion to visual data for enhancing perception systems in autonomous driving. This paper introduces BEVFusion, a straightforward yet robust fusion framework that enables camera features to learn from LiDAR data within a fully end-to-end architecture. The system combines bird's-eye-view (BEV) features from LiDAR and cameras using a dual-branch fusion strategy: a direct branch merges raw BEV features through a simple addition operation, while an indirect branch processes camera BEV features using a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) guided by LiDAR inputs. Our ablation studies demonstrate an average performance improvement of 3.4% across various perception tasks. Furthermore, BEVFusion surpasses recent state-of-the-art methods by 3.1% to 12.5% on the nuScence dataset and achieves state-of-the-art results on Waymo Open Dataset and KITTI. We provide a comprehensive numerical characterization of the thermal profile generated within a liquid by a pump laser, accounting for boundary conditions and the specific laser spatial mode. This approach facilitates the prediction of the spatial-temporal evolution of refractive index perturbations triggered by laser heating. By applying this model to a 4$\pi$ symmetric diffraction experiment involving the absorption of a Gaussian laser by a liquid medium, we demonstrate that the resulting phase object can be accurately simulated. This model is applicable to various scenarios, including the tuning of diffraction patterns and extending numerical simulations to other configurations, such as those utilizing Laguerre-Gaussian modes. Furthermore, the framework can be adapted for other applications, including the parametric amplification of optical vortices. Given that thermal self-induced diffraction is a prevalent phenomenon, our model offers a robust tool for analyzing these effects in both current and future experiments. The accompanying code is freely available. [arXiv:2105.00014v1] [physics.optics] (2021).

Software design discussions are frequently documented in source code comments, commit messages, and pull request descriptions. To leverage these documents for design mining, it is crucial to maintain consistent design names across different artifacts referring to the same element. This paper introduces a technique to assess the stability of such names. The approach involves translating textual statements from a corpus of design-related artifacts into a canonical representation using natural language processing and information retrieval methods. Subsequently, the distance between these canonical representations is calculated to determine stability, with a case study validating the method's effectiveness. This paper expands upon our conference publication [14]. While the conference version focused on the technique's motivation and foundational design, this paper emphasizes validation strategies and explores the technique's applications. Specifically, we demonstrate how the approach supports task automation, including the identification of related design elements and the generation of design name suggestions. Furthermore, we evaluate the technique's applicability within an industrial setting. Our results indicate that while the method is effective, there is room for improvement in the quality of generated design name suggestions. Additionally, we discuss how the proposed technique can be adapted to other domains, such as code search and design migration. The code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchulze1992/ConclusionStability. Our findings suggest that the technique is applicable in industry, and we anticipate that future advancements in design name suggestion will enhance the quality of recommended entities. This study investigates the production of top and bottom partners at the LHC within the composite Higgs framework. We systematically calculate contributions from non-resonant diagrams involving intermediate gluon fusion, making a specific distinction for diagrams where the primary source of composite fermion coupling to the gluon is a fermion loop. These findings are essential for accurately interpreting future LHC searches for top and bottom partners, as well as for establishing limits on the composite Higgs model's parameter space. Our results demonstrate that these non-resonant diagrams can produce significant effects, particularly when the composite Higgs model parameters are not heavily constrained by other analyses. Finally, we provide comprehensive results for LHC Run 3 and Run 4, including projections for a 3 ab$^{-1}$ and 30 ab$^{-1}$ scenarios. Additionally, we have released a python package, CHIDA, designed to facilitate the computation of these diagrams. CHIDAs are derived analytically and integrated into a numerical implementation that is both user-friendly and highly extensible for future applications. Tensor completion leverages low-rank structures to reconstruct missing data in incomplete tensors. While streaming tensor completion algorithms are designed for continuous data streams, they struggle with isolated, sparse samples typical of real-world visual data. This study introduces a novel patch tracking strategy to identify local patch locations within a stream of tensor samples. Additionally, a new streaming tensor ring completion method is developed to recover visual data by exploiting the low-rank characteristics of a constructed patch completion matrix. Experiments on high-resolution incomplete images and video frames demonstrate the method's effectiveness, showing superior performance compared to other solutions. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1993/PatchTracking. Furthermore, the completed images and videos, along with the corresponding incomplete inputs, are available at https://drive.google.

We present numerical simulations of three-dimensional isotropic turbulence within a rotating, inviscid, incompressible framework. In the steeping spectral range, both enstrophy and energy spectra align with the Zakharov-Kolmogorov (ZK) solution [D. Z. Zakharov and V. E. Zakharov, Sov. Phys. JETP 92, 1007 (2000)], a result derived from a perturbative analysis of weak Kelvin wave turbulence under a weak viscosity assumption. By utilizing a high-resolution direct numerical simulation (DNS) approach, we significantly extend the steepening spectral range where the energy spectrum adheres to the ZK spectrum. This analysis examines the validity conditions of the ZK theory and the energy spectrum. Furthermore, we investigate the spectral characteristics of turbulence at high Rossby numbers generated by random forcing, observing the emergence of an inverse energy cascade alongside a $-5/3$ Kolmogorov spectrum. Finally, we offer insights into the non-perturbative energy spectrum at high Reynolds numbers. These findings are achieved through the development of a new high-resolution spectral DNS code. Additionally, we compare these numerical results with experimental data. Our conclusions suggest that the K41 energy spectrum is not universally applicable to all turbulent flows. Consequently, we propose a novel numerical methodology for analyzing energetic turbulent flows. This paper introduces a family of iterative graph normalization techniques, offering a comprehensive characterization of the limit distributions and demonstrating that any deviation from a uniform limit can be explained by the graph's structure. The study also examines various alternative normalization approaches, with a primary emphasis on continuous functions applied to adjacency matrices that preserve symmetry and self-loops. Finally, the work explores the potential of the spectral properties of normalized graphs as a means to approximate maximum weight independent sets. The authors conclude by outlining several open questions regarding the effectiveness and limitations of this approach. This study details a low-frequency monitoring campaign of the M-dwarf binary system CR Draconis, conducted between 2017 and 2019 using the LOFAR Low-Band (LB) and LOFAR Low-Low-Band (LLB) systems. The campaign targeted both quiescent and active phases of the star, with a specific focus on detecting electron-cyclotron maser (EM) emission during flares. We identified 11 flares, with the most prominent event, CR Draconis 20170910, exhibiting a peak flux density of 1.5 mJy at 19 MHz. This emission was localized to the star's position and exhibited a rapid rise and slow decay, peaking at 19.5 MHz. The observed EM radiation displays a power-law temporal profile with a slope of $\alpha \sim 0.75$, a characteristic typical of M-dwarf flares. Analysis of the spectral profile reveals a narrow bandwidth of approximately 100 kHz, indicating a highly collimated electron beam. The spectral shape suggests an electron distribution shaped by a flat-top mechanism, while the frequency evolution points to either a drifting or a single maser cavity. We estimate the maser's altitude to be roughly 1.5 stellar radii, with an initial emission density of $\sim 10^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$. Furthermore, we determined the maser's angular size to be $\sim 0.001$ arcsec, implying a size of $\sim 0.05 R_\odot$. This is the first detection of EM emission from an M dwarf occurring during its quiescent phase. We propose that the quiescent EM signal likely originates from a persistent maser cavity. Additionally, we calculated the flare energy to be $\sim 10^{32}$ erg, consistent with other flares of similar duration. Finally, we estimated the magnetic field strength at the maser site to be between 1.1 and 1.3 kG. These findings suggest that the EM emission arises from a coherent, highly collimated maser process driven by a strong magnetic field. The detection of quiescent EM emission implies that CR Draconis hosts a stable maser cavity, which may be linked to its high binary fraction. These results are crucial for understanding the frequency evolution of EM emission and the dynamics of maser cavities on M dwarfs.

Creating realistic virtual human representations is a core component of human-computer interaction, yet it remains difficult due to the need for time-consuming motion capture sessions and the computational complexity of modeling and animating human bodies. To address these issues, we introduce a novel approach called Articulated Neural Rendering (ANR), which generates virtual human avatars by simultaneously learning the shape and motion of a specific individual. This method requires only a single image of the target person and a library of training avatars to learn local shape variations and global motion patterns. We validate our technique using captured videos of real people to generate virtual versions of their avatars. The resulting avatars can be efficiently and controllably animated with new motions by providing just a skeleton sequence, with shape adjustments made relative to a neutral pose. Furthermore, the generated virtual avatars are capable of reproducing identity-specific features from the input images. Compared to existing articulated neural rendering methods, our approach offers faster training speeds and produces higher-quality virtual avatars. Additionally, the created virtual humans can be rendered in real-time. Experiments confirm that our virtual avatars can be controlled and customized to express various emotions and gestures. Finally, we demonstrate that the virtual humans generated by our method can be swapped into real-world videos and rendered within real-world scenes. The code and datasets will be made publicly available.

The paper investigates the Chern-Simons link invariant within the classical regime ($\hbar=0$), utilizing representation matrices of $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C})$. It demonstrates that the resulting link invariants are essentially governed by the special cases of the Askey-Wilson $q$-hypergeometric series, which correspond to the regular and singular limits of the series. Finally, the paper concludes with several open problems and a bibliography. This work is based on the author's doctoral thesis. Keywords: Chern-Simons theory, Link invariants, Askey-Wilson algebra.

We investigate the thermodynamic characteristics of two-dimensional frustrated trimer antiferromagnets, where each cluster internally forms a singlet ground state. Employing the Edwards-Sanders algorithm for quantum Monte Carlo simulations, we analyze the correlation length, magnetic susceptibility, and specific heat of a square lattice composed of AFM singlet-trimers interacting via either repulsive ($J>0$) or weakly-attractive ($J<0$) potentials. For both repulsive and weakly-attractive scenarios, we identify a phase transition characterized by the emergence of long-range order. Specifically, the magnetic susceptibility and correlation length diverge at a second-order phase transition on a $J<0$ lattice driven by the buildup of long-range order, whereas these quantities exhibit crossovers in the $J>0$ case. We provide a detailed analysis of the second-order transition for $J<0$ and outline the methodology for extracting the critical exponent. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the crossover observed in the $J>0$ case is governed by the fixed point associated with the decoupling of multiple critical modes. Finally, our findings for the $J<0$ regime align with the framework of dimer liquids. This study represents the initial effort to determine the complete phase diagram for this system. Additionally, the techniques developed here are applicable to a broader range of quantum spin systems, including those involving AFM dimers. This work extends the research presented in Ref. [Phys. Large pre-trained language models have demonstrated the ability to perform a broad spectrum of natural language learning tasks without explicit instruction. Nevertheless, their zero-shot capabilities remain constrained, particularly for tasks involving complex query patterns or those with limited training data. This study investigates various methods for enhancing the zero-shot performance of pre-trained models, specifically exploring the adaptation of prompt designs used in prompt-based learning. To achieve this, we introduce the Dataset Adaptation Benchmark (DAB), a collection of 1,000 prompt designs derived from 150 datasets. Our findings indicate that D prompt designs can significantly boost zero-shot results across both individual datasets and the entire benchmark. Furthermore, we observe that the performance of D prompt designs is sensitive to the size of the pre-training dataset. To address this, we evaluate a straightforward yet effective strategy: fine-tuning prompt designs using a small, representative collection of prompt designs. We release this collection, known as Small Instance Dataset Prompt Collection (SIDP), which comprises 100 prompt designs. Finally, we assess the generalizability of both D and SIDP collections on a new benchmark, the Hugging Face Evaluation (HFE), which encompasses prompt designs from 100 models on 100 datasets. Our results demonstrate that pre-training with the SIDP collection yields a substantial performance increase on the HFE benchmark. Additionally, we analyze the relationship between the distribution of prompt designs in these collections and the resulting performance gains. Overall, this work establishes a framework for the efficient adaptation of large pre-trained models for zero-shot learning. This work examines a discrete $Z_3$-invariant Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM) featuring a singlet doublet scenario. We analyze the conditions necessary for a strong first-order electrowewak phase transition (EWPT) and determine the implications for dark matter detection. Additionally, we detail the requirements for detecting gravitational waves generated by this phase transition. In the initial step, we determine the tree-level NMSSM Higgs mass, ensuring the Higgsino mass parameter $\mu$ remains below 1 TeV to facilitate both a strong EWPT and Higgs dark matter detection. Next, we incorporate loop corrections into the Higgs mass calculation. We then apply the conditions for a strong EWPT to the NMSSM parameters and determine the corresponding Higgs mass value. Furthermore, we investigate the possibility of detecting gravitational waves from the phase transition using the LISA detector. Finally, we compare these findings with results from the Higgs coupling sector, direct dark matter searches, and LHC indirect searches. A detailed analysis of the results is provided. Our findings indicate that the NMSSM parameters yielding Higgs dark matter via freeze-in or thermal mechanisms fail to satisfy the strong EWPT condition. Conversely, to achieve a strong EWPT, the light Higgs mass must fall below 1 TeV, and the $\mu$ parameter must be approximately 1 TeV. Under these conditions, the loop-corrected Higgs mass is approximately 125 GeV, aligning with LHC measurements. Additionally, we find that Higgs dark matter detection is feasible, and the phase transition leaves a distinct signature in the power spectrum. Finally, we conclude that the thermal production of a phase transition power spectrum is not viable. However, Higgs dark matter remains a possibility, and the phase transition gravitational wave signal is detectable by LISA. We also note that the power spectrum is sensitive to the reheating temperature, which can be constrained by LHC data. Furthermore, we observe that the reheating temperature is lower than the temperature at which the phase transition occurs. We introduce High-z Sudoku, a diagnostic method designed to evaluate the robustness of (sub)millimeter redshifts. This tool utilizes the "robustness" parameter, which measures the likelihood that a source's redshift remains stable across diverse redshift estimation techniques. The primary objective of High-z Sudoku is to enable researchers to forecast the robustness of their spectroscopic source samples prior to conducting observations. This approach is grounded in the premise that sources identified by coincident detections in multiple spectral lines exhibit the highest confidence in their redshifts. By allowing users to input basic source characteristics, the calculator generates a robustness estimate derived from the expected number of spectral line coincidences. We demonstrate this tool using the publicly available "High-z Sudoku Examples" dataset, which includes sources from the ALMA Redshift Explorer (ALMA-REx) project. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of High-z Sudoku to the upcoming ALMA-REx Cycle 10 observations. Ultimately, High-z Sudoku serves as a valuable resource for (sub)millimeter astronomers, facilitating the planning of observations aimed at determining redshifts for high-redshift galaxies. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ALMA-REx/High-z-Sudoku. We welcome your feedback and encourage you to use the tool. Please note that High-z Sudoku is a diagnostic instrument and does not perform redshift measurements. Consequently, it is not intended to validate the redshifts of existing sources, nor should its output be used to claim the redshifts of any specific source. The robustness estimate reflects the potential for achieving robust redshifts through future observations, contingent upon the source's physical properties. Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, we analyze the string free energy, Polyakov loop correlation functions, and the spectrum of deconfinement-related strings. Our findings indicate that while strings exhibit linear confinement at low temperatures, they display a free energy exponent of $\gamma=1.3$, a value notably higher than the $\gamma=4/3$ predicted by string models for standard $SU(3)$ Yang-Mills or $U(1)$-Higgs theories with $N_f=2$. Furthermore, the string breaking distance is significantly reduced compared to those theories with $N_f=2$ or $N_f=\infty$. We also investigate the correlation function of Polyakov loops along with the string channel spectrum, demonstrating the existence of strings connecting fundamental charges even at temperatures above the deconfinement transition. Finally, our results confirm that the deconfinement transition in this $U(1)$-Higgs model is a first-order phase transition. These outcomes suggest that strings within the deconfined phase are unstable, a feature potentially linked to the presence of strings connecting three charges. This study introduces a kinetic model utilizing a velocity-dependent collision frequency to analyze monatomic rarefied gas flows. The collision frequency is formulated as a low-order expansion in powers of the squared molecular velocity, with coefficients determined by an approximate moment closure. Through numerical simulations of standard benchmark tests, the model's results are compared against the linearized Krüger model, the S-model, the half-range S-model, the Maxwell model, and the exact Boltzmann solution. The findings indicate that this proposed model performs comparably to the S-model and outperforms the S-model, the half-range S-model, the Maxwell model, and the linearized Krüger model across all examined test cases. Furthermore, the model demonstrates the ability to capture third-order effects of the intermolecular potential, a capability that the S-model and the half-range S-model lack. Finally, the model is applied to simulate a rarefied gas flow past a sphere at a Knudsen number of 10, yielding results that align well with the exact Boltzmann solution. These results suggest that the model remains effective for this external flow scenario and retains potential for application to more complex configurations. The model's simplicity and favorable performance make it a strong candidate for use in multiscale simulations of rarefied gas flows. Additionally, the model is readily extendable to polyatomic gases by incorporating an appropriate collision frequency alongside internal degrees of freedom. This approach offers a significant advantage over the S-model, which relies on a relaxation-time approximation that is less accurate for molecular gases. The paper concludes with a discussion of the model's potential for further development. Finally, this work serves as a foundation for the companion study, which examines an application to a complex, multiscale flow scenario. In that companion work, the S-model is shown to be inadequate for accurately representing third-order intermolecular potential effects, whereas the proposed model successfully achieves this. Consequently, the collision frequency derived here is utilized in the subsequent paper to develop a more sophisticated model for polyatomic rarefied gas flows. The upcoming Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) aims to investigate the internal structure of protons and nuclei, as well as hard scattering processes within their hadronic components. To achieve this, the EIC will conduct high-precision, high-luminosity measurements of open charm and bottom hadrons. This presentation will outline the design and development of the Forward Silicon Tracker (FST), a device intended to measure the momentum of these heavy flavor hadrons in the very forward region of the collider. Additionally, we will examine the detector's performance and the data analysis techniques required to isolate the rare signals of heavy hadrons against a significant light-flavor background. The FST is being designed and developed by a consortium of institutions from the US, UK, and Europe. Specifically, this talk represents the perspective of the experimental group from the Fermilab Transformations Office, which is contributing to the tracker's development. This work builds upon our prior experience with the Fermilab Meson Program (fMP), a high-rate, real-time R&D initiative for high-granularity silicon tracking detectors. Through the fMP, we have successfully demonstrated the entire end-to-end process of high-rate online event selection, fast digitization, data acquisition, and real-time heavy-flavor hadron reconstruction. Furthermore, we will showcase recent results from an FST-like detector tested at Fermilab's PIP-3 test stand. These findings will inform the design of the FST for the EIC. The PIP-3 tests utilized a silicon tracker featuring 100 layers of 200 $\mu$m thick double-sided pixel sensors, offering a high granularity of 0.15 x 0.2 mm$^2$ per readout pad. This sensor geometry mirrors the final design planned for the EIC's FST. The talk will also address the integration of advanced data analysis techniques, including machine learning, into the online event selection and event reconstruction processes. Finally, we will present results from a recent FST prototype equipped with a real-time online data acquisition system, demonstrating its performance in identifying J/$\psi$ $\to$ $\mu^+\mu^-$ decays. This study examines the photometric variability of the low-mass active galactic nucleus (AGN) SDSS J1030+0524, utilizing a comprehensive dataset of optical photometry collected between 2011 and 2017. The source exhibits significant fluctuations in both quiescent and variable brightness, with the latter attributed to the recurrent emergence of new transient events. We identify a notable event occurring between 2014 and 2015, characterized by a 1.5 magnitude increase in quiescent brightness, which we classify as an eruption. Furthermore, the variability observed during the pre- and post-eruptive phases is analyzed through the lens of stochastic accretion and oscillation models. Our findings indicate that stochastic accretion is the primary driver of the pre- and post-eruptive variability, while oscillation remains a viable alternative explanation. Additionally, we establish a minimum quiescent accretion rate of $\dot{M} \gtrsim 10^{-3} \dot{M}_{Edd}$, a conclusion that holds regardless of the specific variability mechanism. Finally, we compare the pre- and post-eruptive light curves to investigate the long-term impact of the eruption on the AGN's variability. The post-eruptive light curve displays a higher dispersion in fractional flux variations compared to the pre-eruptive phase, a trend that may suggest a delayed effect from the eruption. This study presents spectropolarimetric observations of HD58260, a rapidly rotating, metal-poor A0V star, conducted using the ESPaDOnS instrument on the CFHT. The primary objective was to detect magnetic field fields in the stellar atmosphere by analyzing emission lines of neutral metals in the near-ultraviolet range. We identified clear longitudinal magnetic field signals in the presence of significant activity, including activity-induced variability and bisector inversions. By employing the Inversion of the Cross-Correlation (IvCross) method, we derived mean longitudinal magnetic field values of $-120 \pm 10$ G and $-130 \pm 10$ G, which align with values from prior studies. Furthermore, we identified numerous individual lines exhibiting strong circular polarization and moderate to strong linear polarization, indicating that these lines are formed in regions with varying magnetic field strengths. Specifically, emission lines such as Fe i 2024.05, Fe i 2024.15, and Fe i 2024.25, which are typically formed in the upper photosphere or low chromosphere, displayed the strongest polarization signals. By comparing these lines with absorption lines formed deeper in the atmosphere, we observed that the upper atmospheric layers possess a magnetic field strength approximately 1.5 times stronger than the deeper layers. This finding supports the hypothesis that the magnetic field strength increases toward the stellar surface. Additionally, we observed a correlation between the intensity of circular polarization and the degree of emission in these lines. Finally, we demonstrated that the emission component in these lines is not solely caused by the scattering of photospheric light by chromospheric plasma but also stems from the excitation of upper levels by photons emitted from the magnetic field. These results offer the first direct evidence of a magnetic field gradient within the atmosphere of a rapidly rotating metal-poor star. These observations also indicate the presence of a magnetic field in the stellar atmosphere, a phenomenon previously detected only in cooler stars. The observed gradient may contribute to the heating of the chromosphere and corona, as well as the generation of a magnetic braking mechanism. Future observations of other stars with ESPaOnS and NIRPS will aim to confirm this phenomenon across different spectral types and investigate its impact on stellar activity. These findings may also help explain the discrepancies between the observed and predicted spin-down of rapidly rotating stars. We present ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ recombination line in the low-metallicity galaxy NGC 5253, covering a 1.5 kpc scale with a spatial resolution of 10 pc. These observations reveal a compact, centrally concentrated star-forming region with a diameter of approximately 1 kpc, characterized by a mean H30$\alpha$ surface brightness of 0.15 Jy/beam. This surface brightness corresponds to a mean H30$\alpha$ luminosity of roughly 1.5 L$_{\odot}$ per 100 pc$^2$, which aligns with the value predicted by the Kennicutt-Schmidt law for H3$\alpha$ emission. The H30$\alpha$ emission is primarily driven by massive stars with masses exceeding 20 M$_{\odot}$, which also generate significant amounts of H2 and dust. Consequently, the H30$\alpha$ line serves as a reliable tracer for both star formation rates and rates within 100 pc scales. We conducted a detailed comparison between the H30$\alpha$-derived star formation rate and the galaxy's star formation rate derived from its color-magnitude relation, finding them to be in good agreement. Furthermore, we compared the H30$\alpha$ surface brightness distribution with the galaxy's dust distribution, observing that the dust emission is more extended than the H30$\alpha$ emission. This discrepancy is attributed to the fact that dust is produced by both massive stars and lower-mass stars (M$<$20 M$_{\odot}$). Finally, we tested two recently proposed star formation rate metrics against the H30$\alpha$ data, confirming that the new metric (SFR$_{new}$) correlates more strongly with H30$\alpha$ surface brightness than the traditional Kennicutt-Schmidt metric (SFR$_{Kennicutt}$) does. These findings suggest that SFR$_{new}$ is a more effective tool for characterizing star formation in galaxies. The data will be accessible via the NRO ALMA archive (project code 2019.1.00005.L). This study addresses the development of reduced-order and high-gain observers for a specific epidemic model. We demonstrate the existence of these observers and provide their gain matrices. Additionally, we simulate the observer performance to validate our theoretical findings. Our motivation stems from a recent effort to construct a reduced-order observer for a recently introduced extended S-I-R epidemic process that incorporates hospitalization and death rates alongside the standard infection and recovery dynamics. While we successfully designed a reduced-order observer for this recently proposed model, extending this approach to other epidemiological models remains an open challenge. The objective of this work is to evaluate the performance of reduced-order and high-gain observers across various well-known S-I-R model variants. Specifically, we analyze the most commonly used versions of these models in the literature. Our results indicate that both observer types exhibit satisfactory performance for the model under consideration. Furthermore, we show that reduced-order observers yield excellent estimates for model parameters, whereas high-gain observers provide accurate estimates for nonlinear infection rates of the form $\beta(I)I$ and $\beta I^m$. These findings may assist researchers in estimating parameters for the specific epidemic model or other related frameworks. Additionally, our methodology offers a straightforward and efficient alternative for parameter estimation in other S-I-R epidemic models. Finally, we note that reduced-order observers are not limited to S-I-R type models; they can also be applied to other dynamical systems.

Keywords: State estimation, epidemic processes, observer design, parameter estimation.

Integrating temporal information into knowledge graph embedding (KGE) has recently become a significant research area, with recent studies demonstrating that incorporating temporal models enhances performance on specific queries. However, this trend is less pronounced in link prediction tasks within temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs). We contend that tertain static models yield promising results in specific Link Prediction scenarios inside TKGs. This paper aims to investigate the applicability of static models in tese scenarios and explore methods for leveraging them within TTKGs. To achieve this, we employ a multi-task learning approach that utilizes time slices and lops temporal models. We evaluate our method against ten KGE baselines across four real-world datasets, showing that it achieves state-of-the-art performance in Link Prediction on two of them. Furthermore, we present an analysis of results and provide insights to guide the selection of appropriate models for these tasks. Ultrashort pulse lasers are essential for numerous applications, yet their development is often hindered by the complexity of the underlying physics. This study introduces a geometrical analysis of Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLML) that elucidates the stability and performance of the stabilization technique. By employing ABCD matrix formalism, we derive closed-form expressions for key parameters, including cavity dispersion, pulse energy, pulse duration, pulse position within the stabilizing cavity, and the lensing strength of the Kerr effect. Furthermore, we present a phase-space diagram to visualize stable and unstable operating regions. These findings are supported by experimental data from a 100-fs Ti:sapphire KLML laser. The paper offers a comprehensive overview of the stabilization method, accompanied by mathematical derivations and numerical results. Ultimately, the proposed analysis serves as a valuable tool for designing and analyzing high-peak-power ultrafast oscillators. Additionally, the generalization of this analysis to other stabilization techniques is discussed. This work is designed to be accessible to students and researchers across various fields. This paper introduces a novel Resource-Aware asynchronous online federated learning (RA-FL) framework designed to enhance the efficiency of asynchronous online federated learning (AOFL) algorithms in nonlinear regression. To boost computational efficiency, the study examines the relationship between the number of local updates and model accuracy. Building upon the SOA-AOFL algorithm, RA-AOFL is developed by dynamically adjusting the local update frequency based on resource availability at client devices. Theoretically, the convergence properties of the proposed RA-AOFL algorithm are established, and simulation results demonstrate that this approach achieves a significant improvement in computational efficiency. Furthermore, experiments on real-world datasets validate the method's effectiveness. Additionally, the research explores the trade-off between model performance and computational efficiency, offering practical guidance for deploying machine learning models. The optical absorption characteristics of thin silicon films are significantly improved through the use of 3D photonic band gap (3D-PBG) materials as back reflectors. By functioning as high-quality Fabry-Perot resonators, these structures induce strong local field enhancements within the silicon layer, thereby boosting absorption. This performance surpasses that of silicon backed by conventional 2D photonic crystal reflectors, which rely on diffractive scattering into guided modes. The study provides a detailed analysis of the absorption spectra for thin silicon films supported by 3D-PBG structures, alongside an investigation into the optimal design parameters. Furthermore, these 3D-PBG backed reflectors are demonstrated to be effective in ultra-thin silicon films used as absorbers in thin-film solar cells. The research concludes by identifying the critical design requirements necessary to maximize absorption in such thin film configurations. Additionally, the potential of these 3D-PBG backed reflectors to substantially enhance absorption in ultra-thin silicon films, intended for other applications, is briefly explored. The entire study was conducted using a full-wave finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulation method. Finally, the authors outline the primary challenges associated with the fabrication of these 3D-PBG structures. We introduce a novel construction of high-dimensional expanders (HDXs) utilizing covering spaces of finite groups. We present a criterion ensuring that this hierarchy-based construction preserves HDX properties and maintainability across levels, which is applied to create a new family of linear spaces HDXs. Additionally, we offer an application to inverse eigenvalue problems within the context of high-dimensional expanders. The paper includes a comprehensive tutorial on these problems, featuring new results alongside existing ones. Furthermore, we utilize our criterion to construct higher-dimensional expanders by adapting methods from other areas, such as Saraf-Wootters' work on quantum LDPC codes. Finally, we demonstrate that our method can produce fractional dimensional expanders, which are defined as graphs with spectral expansion. Throughout the study, we emphasize the role of higher homology. Our findings are motivated by the observation that many current HDX constructions rely on cosets of subgroups within finite groups, which often result in poor parameter performance. Our approach addresses this by working with the groups themselves rather than their cosets. The paper is structured into two sections: the first presents our mathematical results, while the second outlines our computational results, which were developed in collaboration with various researchers. The study investigates the magnetic characteristics of the Gd$^{3+}$-based perovskite antiferromagnet GdInO$_3$ (GIO) using bulk magnetization and muon spin rotation ($\mu$SR) techniques. Magnetization data indicate a second-order antiferromagnetic phase transition at $T_{\rm N}=3.25$ K, with a linear temperature dependence of magnetization above this point. However, $\mu$SR experiments reveal that muons implanted in GIO do not detect an ordered magnetic field at $T_{\rm N}$, suggesting that only a small fraction of Gd$^{3+}$ ions order. This is corroborated by magnetization results, which show a maximum bulk ordered moment of $\mu_{\rm eff}^{\rm ord}=0.95\pm0.05\,\mu_{\rm B}$, corresponding to approximately 10% of the total Gd$^{3+}$ ions. The $\mu$SR data further indicate a highly anisotropic magnetic structure where the ordered moment is oriented perpendicular to the $ab$-plane. We propose a microscopic model consistent with these findings, which attributes the partial magnetic ordering to strong dipole-dipole interactions between Gd$^{3+}$ ions within the same layer. This model also accounts for the observed divergence between bulk magnetization and $\mu$SR findings and explains the lack of a significant kink in the electrical resistivity at $T_{\rm N}$. Additionally, the magnetic structure is found to be sensitive to the applied field direction, exhibiting a cusp-like anomaly in the field-cooled magnetization curve at $H_{\rm ext}=1.5$ kOe when the field is applied parallel to the $c$-axis. Finally, we demonstrate that a classical Heisenberg model, featuring nearest-neighbor interactions within layers and next-to-nearest-neighbor interactions between layers, can qualitatively reproduce the experimental observations. The derived exchange parameters suggest that the magnetic structure is nearly uniaxial, with the easy axis aligned along the $c$-axis. This is attributed to the interplay between exchange interactions and a weak magnetocrystalline anisotropy arising from the non-collinear arrangement of the GdInO$_3$ unit cells. Graph embedding has emerged as a highly effective method for link prediction, yet most existing approaches concentrate on dense networks, leaving sparse ones largely unaddressed. This paper introduces Sparse-SNE (SSNE), a novel node representation technique designed specifically for link prediction in sparse network topologies. SSNE employs a two-stage strategy: first, it identifies and retains a set of informative neighbors for each node, followed by the generation of a low-dimensional representation. This neighbor selection process is critical to SSNE's success, enabling it to achieve a 10% to 20% improvement in link prediction accuracy over current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we validate SSNE's efficacy across various real-world sparse networks, including those found in social media, biological systems, and computer networks. The implementation code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/ChenchenLi1998/Ssne}. Additionally, this work is expanded upon in our survey chapter, \textit{Sparse Networks: A Survey}, within the book \textit{Encyclopedia of Social Media}, published by Springer. We present a new class of atomic vapor cells featuring an integrated, multi-layered silicon micro-structure designed to enhance atom-fluid interactions. This design utilizes a deep silicon micro-channel, manufactured via deep reactive ion etching, to host the atomic vapor. A silicon film, deposited through physical vapor deposition and patterned using deep ultraviolet lithography, acts as an optical window. By employing this micro-fabrication approach, we created a compact cell measuring 1.5 mm in width and 10 mm in length, capable of sustaining a sodium atom density of 10^{13} cm^{-3} at approximately 175°C. This device supports high optical transmission rates of 90% at 589 nm. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the silicon window can be removed to facilitate vapor injection, enabling the construction of a configurable optical setup. This configuration is optimized for applications such as atomic magnetometers and atomic vapor quantum memories. Additionally, we illustrate that these silicon-based vapor cells can be seamlessly integrated into broader micro-fabricated electronic systems, including integrated circuit chipsets and solid-state lasers. This capability significantly simplifies the production of atomic vapor-assisted photonic devices and opens avenues for developing complex atomic systems on a single chip. Finally, we highlight the potential for creating large-scale atomic systems by connecting multiple micro-fabricated vapor cells. Such a network could support advanced applications like distributed atomic magnetometry and atomic force microscopy. This work establishes a foundation for the future widespread use of atomic vapor systems in integrated electronic and photonic devices. The resulting silicon-based vapor cells are expected to be essential components in the emerging field of integrated atomic systems. Wildfires pose a significant threat to human life and the environment, making their early detection crucial for mitigation. While deep learning has proven effective for object detection, it often struggles with small targets and low-resolution imagery. To address this, we introduce a deep learning-based infrared-visible (IR-VIS) data fusion technique designed to enhance wildfire detection in low-resolution scenarios. This novel approach utilizes a multi-stream encoder-decoder deep learning architecture to generate fused images that are superior to raw data for identifying dispersed fires. The method employs a spatial attention mechanism to emphasize relevant features and a multi-stream encoder-decoder structure to extract features from both IR and VIS inputs. Extensive experiments were conducted to validate the fusion algorithm's efficacy. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches, achieving a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 0.821 on the Wildfire-100 dataset. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar1999/FIRe-GAN.

This study presents the creation of the "Signs of Depression" dataset, assembled from Twitter posts by individuals diagnosed with depression. The collection process involved identifying Twitter handles from medical records and monitoring these specific users over a six-month period. From the resulting six-month data, 2,000 tweets were manually chosen and categorized into four classes: "Signs of Depression," "Not a Sign of Depression," "Ambiguous," and "Others." Following this, 500 tweets were randomly selected from each category for the training set, while an additional 500 tweets from each category were reserved for testing. The analysis employed a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier, which achieved a classification accuracy of 80%. These findings indicate that text classification is a viable approach for identifying indicators of depression in social media content. The dataset and associated analysis code are publicly accessible at: https://github.com/rajkumar2000/Depression-Detection. Future research will explore the application of Natural Language Processing techniques to further enhance classification accuracy. This work was conducted while the first author was a visiting scholar at the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, IIT Guwahati. The corresponding author's affiliation will be updated to reflect their position at the University of the West Indies, Cave Hill, following their upcoming move. Keywords: Depression Detection, Text Classification, SVM, NLP.

Furthermore, for scenarios where the infection rate aligns with the susceptible population size, the model demonstrates equivalent dynamics to an SIRS-type model, indicating a transition from an infected state back to a susceptible state. Finally, the paper examines the conditions required for the convergence of this stochastic model toward the original deterministic one. This study investigates the influence of isoscalar quadrupole-strength coupling on isoscalar monopole strength within $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si, specifically regarding the isoscalar monopole strength sum rule. Utilizing the relativistic quasiparticle random-phase approximation, we computed the energy-weighted monopole strength sum rule, accounting for the effects of quadrupole coupling. Our results indicate that this coupling significantly impacts the sum rule in $^{24}$Mg but has a negligible effect in $^{28}$Si. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that this phenomenon can be understood through single-particle properties, which are derived from the relativistic mean-field potential. Finally, we analyze the implications of these findings for future experiments. This work serves as a precursor to our investigation of quadrupole coupling in the isoscalar monopole strength sum rule for $^{40}$Ca, $^{48}$Ca, and $^{208}$Pb. The theoretical framework employed is grounded in our prior research on monopole strength sum rules in $^{40}$Ca and $^{208}$Pb. Additionally, we explore the relationship between monopole strength sum rules and monopole moments. The calculations were conducted using the CH88 parameter set. This work investigates stick-slip phenomena and trajectory convergence in feedback-controlled motion systems featuring Coulomb friction, alongside numerical approaches for approximating solution sets. The Coulomb friction coefficient is modeled as a piecewise-constant function dependent on the system's trajectory. Consequently, the friction-affected tracking task is framed as a hybrid system problem, yielding a hybrid feedback control law. This law comprises a conventional continuous component for standard motion and a binary control component to manage the switching dynamics arising from Coulomb friction. For the resulting hybrid closed-loop system, we demonstrate local exponential convergence of trajectories to the desired reference, with the control demonstrating robustness against perturbations. Furthermore, we establish that the tracking error remains bounded despite uncertainties in the Coulomb friction coefficient. Finally, we present set-valued approaches to characterize the set of all potential solutions for the arising hybrid control problem, supported by numerical examples. These solutions may involve sliding on the sliding surface, where the control becomes discontinuous. Such solutions are well-defined within the framework of Filippov solutions or Sliding Mode Control theory. Additionally, sliding modes emerge at the switching points of Coulomb force direction, creating sliding segments that form part of the system's trajectory. We address the challenge of sliding modes by proposing the computation of equivalent continuous control, which facilitates the approximation of the solution set. Equipped with this solution set, the tracking error can be minimized by selecting appropriate approximations. However, the non-smooth nature of Coulomb friction precludes the use of standard sliding mode theory; therefore, we develop a novel framework for sliding mode analysis within hybrid systems. This approach enables the derivation of sliding modes and the assessment of sliding mode stability. Our methodology is applicable to a broader class of hybrid systems than the specific Coulomb friction case. To validate the approach, we provide a numerical example of a friction-affected tracking task with unknown Coulomb friction coefficients, solved using the proposed method. This case study confirms the solution set's robustness regarding parameter uncertainty. Additionally, it demonstrates that the error bound is significantly smaller than the uncertainty in the Coulomb friction coefficient. Crucially, the proposed solution set approach offers a more efficient alternative to sliding mode approximations, as it avoids the need to calculate the reaching law. This efficiency is particularly advantageous when dealing with sliding modes of infinite duration. The solution set encompasses all potential solutions, including those exhibiting sliding modes. Recent studies have shown that traditional hedging strategies fail to achieve near-optimal performance in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) due to the Bellman bias inherent in function approximation. To address this, the Deep Bellman Hedge (DBH) algorithm was introduced, which adaptively balances between the classical Bellman framework and a trained function to correct Bellman errors. This paper extends the analysis of the episodic DBH algorithm to a more general, non-stationary context. We subsequently propose a novel algorithm, Episodic Deep Bellman Hedging with Function Adaptation (EDBHF), which integrates function adaptation into the process. Theoretical analysis confirms the convergence of this new algorithm, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art reinforcement learning methods. Notably, EDBHF is the first algorithm to achieve an overall win rate exceeding 90% across a broad spectrum of challenging scenarios. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/Chenchen-Z/DeepBellmanHedge}. Furthermore, the method has been successfully applied to solve a real-world inventory management problem. This indicates that the proposed approach is highly effective for many practical applications. The results also suggest that function adaptation is a viable strategy for addressing non-stationarity in reinforcement learning. Finally, our work underscores the value of developing theoretical analyses for function-approximation-based hedging techniques. By providing a theoretical foundation, these analyses can guide the design of future hedging methods. The theoretical insights also offer a potential pathway for achieving convergence guarantees in other function-approximation techniques, such as the widely used $\epsilon$-greedy method. Sequential recommender systems are designed to suggest items to users based on their past consumption history. However, this approach faces a significant limitation: it can only recommend items the user has not yet consumed, thereby excluding popular items that are central to the user's current interests. To address this, we propose SEPIA, a sequential recommender system enhanced with an interpretable model of user intent derived from consumption sequences. This model identifies the key intents behind a user's recent activity and recommends items aligned with those specific intents. We evaluated the system using both online and offline metrics across three datasets. The results demonstrate that our method effectively balances the recommendation of high-quality, relevant items with high popularity. Furthermore, the user-interpreted model scores consistently correlate with system performance on all metrics, confirming the interpretability of the proposed approach. Additionally, we find that the distribution of high-performing items in our recommendations is more uniform compared to those of existing sequential recommender systems. The reducible double confluent Heun equation (DCHE) stands as the unique DCHE for which the general symmetric unfolding of the origin (GSUO) is defined. This paper investigates the reducible DCHE specifically within the context of this unfolding. We derive the general monodromy group associated with the GSUO and establish a deficiency theorem. Additionally, we present a deficiency criterion for this specific equation. We also formulate the necessary and sufficient conditions under which the equation possesses a regular singular point, thereby enabling the reduction of the Heun equation to the confluent hypergeometric equation through a shift of the origin. Furthermore, we identify the conditions required for the existence of a second kind solution that decays at infinity. Finally, we provide a criterion for the existence of algebraic solutions in the case where the equation is not reducible to the confluent hypergeometric equation via shifting the origin. These findings are achieved through the development of a new method for deriving indicial equations and a novel approach to the indicial equation method. These results are applicable to the general symmetric unfolding of the origin. Additionally, we explore the connection between the reducible DCHE and the general Heun equation. In this process, we introduce a novel unfolding of the Heun equation, the general Heun equation at three points, and the Heun equation. We demonstrate that the reducible DCHE is a sub-case of the general Heun equation at three points and a further sub-case of the Heun equation. A key outcome of this work is a new criterion for the existence of algebraic solutions to the Heun equation and the Heun equation at three points. These findings also extend to the general DCHE and the GSUO. Our methodology is based on the "shift trick," a technique previously employed in the study of the Heun equation. We anticipate that these results will be valuable for the theory of Heun equations. This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 11771015). Low-rank matrix recovery is a core challenge in statistics and machine learning, with applications spanning collaborative filtering, phase retrieval, and multi-factor investment. This study examines the asymptotic mean squared error risk of the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) in the context of recovering a rank-one matrix from noisy observations characterized by groupwise heteroskedasticity. The analysis reveals a sharp asymptotic phase transition that delineates the risk behavior of the MLE. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a simple, easily implementable estimator, which incorporates a data-driven noise model, achieves this minimal risk. Consequently, this proposed method surpasses the minimax lower bound established in prior literature. Additionally, we establish that the MLE is asymptotically normal when the local risk converges to the minimax lower bound, and we derive a detection-error exponent for the asymptotically optimal hypothesis test. Finally, simulations conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that our estimator outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches. Although most symmetry topological models depend on a symmetry to safeguard their symmetry-protected or crystalline nature, we introduce a symmetry-independent intrinsic topological framework grounded in K-theory. Notably, this model remains robust against anemone-like deformations in configuration space and external symmetries, relying solely on the intrinsic characteristics of the Hamiltonian. We derive the intrinsic symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase from the intrinsic K-theory group $\widehat{K}_0^{in}$ and validate this approach using the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model. Furthermore, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between the intrinsic topological phase and the standard symmetry-topological phase within $\widehat{K}_0^{in}$ and the conventional symmetry-based $\widehat{K}_1^{sym}$ groups. Finally, we demonstrate that the intrinsic topological phase can be induced without breaking any symmetries by manipulating the system's parameters. This research offers a novel perspective on intrinsic topological phases and their potential to expand the landscape of topological matter. Additionally, the proposed intrinsic model and framework are anticipated to be applicable to the intrinsic topological phases of various other fundamental systems in both one and higher dimensions. We introduce a new semi-inclusive lepton flavor universality (LFU) ratio designed for experiments at Belle II and LUCC. This ratio is constructed from the $\mu^+\mu^-$ and $e^+e^-$ decay lepton energy spectra integrated over all other kinematic variables. This approach offers significant benefits: it demands low statistics for validation and allows for the control of certain systematic uncertainties that typically hinder LFU tests in exclusive decays. Furthermore, this ratio can be validated using LFU in $B\to D\ell\nu$ decays, which are currently the most sensitive probes of LFU violations in charged current transitions. We also examine the ratio within the framework of the minimal $\Delta F=2$ model. This framework predicts deviations from the Standard Model in $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions that are comparable in magnitude but opposite in sign, a scenario potentially testable by Belle II. Finally, we present the first all-order perturbative QCD predictions for the ratio, incorporating $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^2)$ corrections for the inclusive decay $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$. These predictions are expected to be accurate to the per mille level. Our numerical analysis indicates that the ratio can be measured with a precision of approximately $1\%$ at Belle II, which is sufficient to detect the predicted deviations from the Standard Model. This measurement will be achievable once the data sample reaches $50~\mathrm{ab}^{-1}$. At LUCC, the precision is expected to improve to roughly $0.1\%$ with $1~\mathrm{ab}^{-1}$ of data. The systematic uncertainties associated with this ratio are primarily systematic in nature, with statistical systematics playing a secondary role. Consequently, the ratio is highly susceptible to systematic effects arising from the modeling of the $b\to u$ sector, which is currently the limiting factor for its sensitivity. We estimate the systematic uncertainty to be around $1\%$ for $50~\mathrm{ab}^{-1}$ at Belle II and $0.1\%$ for $1~\mathrm{ab}^{-1}$ at LUCC. These systematic uncertainties are expected to be reducible in the near future. This paper introduces a decentralized control strategy for linear time-invariant systems featuring multiple communication channels, where each channel is assigned to a specific controller. A key advantage of this approach is that every controller requires only local state information from its designated channel. The primary challenge in designing such a scheme is ensuring stability without relying on global system data. By applying a generalized version of the small gain theorem, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for stability in decentralized linear systems, expressed through the spectral radius of a matrix that depends exclusively on individual channel properties. Consequently, this enables the local design and implementation of decentralized control schemes. We also present an algorithm for gain scheduling, allowing controllers to adapt their gains in response to variations in system or network parameters. This design facilitates a plug-and-play capability: when a new subsystem joins the network, its local controller can be synthesized in real-time using a simple algorithm that needs no knowledge of the overall system. A simulation example demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed method. The stability conditions and the connection to distributed model predictive control are subsequently illustrated through examples and applications. Finally, we relate our findings to recent research on decentralized control. The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread fear and significant loss of life, prompting a surge in the development of diagnostic tools. While researchers have created various methods to classify whether an individual is infected, the need to distinguish between patients with and without lung complications remains critical for determining appropriate treatment. This study introduces a novel two-stage deep learning framework that leverages BERT features to address both classification tasks. In each stage, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) processes the BERT model's output features to generate predictions. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed framework outperforms existing methods, achieving accuracy scores of 99.00% for positive classification and 98.40% for complicated cases. Additionally, the study confirms the robustness of the proposed approach. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first application of BERT features and a two-stage CNN architecture to pandemic classification. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/abdullahkaya1992/Two-Stage-Deep-Learning-Classification-using-BERT-Features}. Furthermore, the authors have released a Python package for the two-stage classification framework, which is available on PyPI at \url{https://pypi.org/project/Two-Stage-Deep-Learning/}. This package includes a convolutional function that accepts a BERT model and image-shaped data as inputs and returns a classification output. By importing this package, researchers can build their own classification models that utilize BERT features. The Python package is licensed under the MIT License. The authors hope that this resource will facilitate the development of new models for pandemic classification that employ BERT features. Additionally, the package serves as a foundation for creating transferable models for other diseases. Given the growing demand for medical image analysis, the two-stage framework described herein is expected to see increased adoption. We anticipate that this resource will contribute to the advancement of deep learning applications in medical image analysis. The field of eco-evolutionary dynamics investigates how ecological and evolutionary processes interact across various spatial, temporal, and hierarchical scales. Typically, these systems are governed by ecological timescales (days to years) and shorter evolutionary rates (generations to centuries). However, the interplay between these domains is complex and scale-dependent. Specifically, ecological and evolutionary dynamics are significantly influenced by the variation in their respective rates, driven by factors such as population sizes, spatial heterogeneity, and environmental variability. Consequently, our understanding of these systems relies heavily on modeling approaches that capture eco-evolutionary timescale interactions and the mechanisms regulating the speeds of ecological and evolutionary change. This review examines the eco-evolutionary timescale, its dependencies, and the underlying mechanisms through a synthesis of both mathematical and experimental perspectives. We outline the theoretical basis for timescale variation and the factors driving it, supported by experimental data demonstrating how fluctuating environmental conditions can alter ecological and evolutionary rates. Furthermore, we present a conceptual framework to illustrate how these changes impact system dynamics, with potential applications ranging from disease control to conservation. Finally, we discuss the challenges inherent in eco-evolutionary research and propose future directions for this emerging field. By integrating mathematical theory with experimental evidence, we aim to inspire a renewed focus on the timescales governing eco-evolutionary systems. Ultimately, we contend that timescale interactions are a fundamental aspect of eco-evolutionary research, and that theoretical and experimental investigations into these interactions are essential for advancing our understanding of ecology and evolution. The speech community is increasingly adopting self-supervised learning (SSL) models, which are largely unsupervised, to develop automatic speech processing tools. Nevertheless, the adversarial susceptibility of these SSL models remains poorly understood. This study investigates the adversarial weaknesses of speech SSL models across various architectures and training methods. Our findings indicate that adversarial attacks succeed with high probability against speech SSL models, regardless of their specific architecture or training protocol. Furthermore, we demonstrate that speech SSL models trained using only supervised learning are more vulnerable than those combining self-supervised and supervised training. Additionally, the speed of SSL model training does not significantly influence their adversarial robustness. Finally, we observe that speech SSL models are susceptible to gradient masking, a phenomenon that complicates the assessment of their true adversarial resilience. These results offer valuable insights for future research aimed at enhancing the robustness of speech processing systems. The code and experiments are accessible at https://github.com/robinson123456789/SSL-attacks. The data utilized in this study can be found at https://drive.google.

This study examines the market dynamics of a blockchain-based decentralized exchange (DEX) where the trading volume of a specific asset pair influences the transaction costs for both participants. We construct a theoretical framework involving two traders and two types of brokers: traditional brokers offer cost-independent services, while blockchain-based DEX providers incur costs determined by the cumulative trading volume of all users. We analyze two scenarios: one where both traders interact with the same broker, and another where they can choose between two different brokers. Our findings indicate that traditional brokers are most advantageous when only one trader is involved, as they can charge a higher cost than DEX providers. However, with two traders, traditional brokers are optimal only if the trading costs between them would be higher than those offered by a DEX. Consequently, traditional brokers are likely to be supplanted by blockchain-based DEX providers. Additionally, we observe that the probability of a blockchain-based broker being the optimal choice rises as the volume sensitivity increases. Finally, we validate these insights through a numerical simulation. In this simulation, two traders select between two types of brokers, each incurring a trading volume cost that scales with the total volume from both users. We measure the likelihood that blockchain-based brokers are optimal under various sensitivity conditions, confirming that this probability increases as sensitivity grows. Furthermore, we evaluate the impact of the trading volume discount on transaction utility, finding that higher sensitivity leads to greater utility. These results align with our theoretical analysis. Sensitivity analysis serves as a framework for examining how conclusions from empirical research change under varying assumptions regarding the data generation process. This is particularly crucial in contexts involving missing data, where inferences are drawn from incomplete samples, and the value at risk increases with the proportion of missing information. We introduce an approach to missing data sensitivity analysis grounded in Bayesian model checking, utilizing the E-value as a metric for the magnitude of effect-size deviations. By integrating model comparison with posterior evaluation, we define regions of interest to identify robust features. In sensitivity analyses, the focus shifts from distinguishing models to quantifying the strength of assumptions; consequently, we assess the posterior probability that a specific assumption holds true. To demonstrate this method, we apply it to two distinct missing-data scenarios: first, a simple missing-at-random scenario with a single missing variable, and second, a more complex missing-not-at-random scenario involving multiple missing variables and a selection model. For both cases, we employ the TITEFSN package to conduct the analyses. Finally, we illustrate how this framework can inform robust inference. The ALICE experiment at the LHC has measured the combined prompt and non-prompt (originating from b-hadron decays) $D^0$ meson nuclear modification factor, denoted as $R_{AA}$, within the transverse momentum range of $2 < p_T < 10$ GeV/$c$ at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV for central Pb-Pb collisions. This result is compared against measurements of purely prompt $D^0$ mesons in $p$-Pb and pp collisions, as well as against purely non-prompt $D^0$ mesons in Pb-W collisions. Additionally, a measurement of the $D^0$ $AA$ ratio restricted exclusively to purely prompt $D^0$ mesons in Pb-Pb collisions is presented. The $R_{AA}$ values for both non-prompt and prompt $D^0$ mesons in Pb-Pb collisions are notably higher than those observed in similar $p_T$ intervals at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=2.76$ TeV. Furthermore, the $R_{AA}$ for non-prompt $D^0$ mesons in Pb-Pb collisions is approximately 1.5 times greater than that of prompt $D^0$ mesons, a difference that persists across all $p_T$ values. This finding contradicts the hypothesis that both populations experience identical medium effects, suggesting either a significantly longer path length for non-prompt $D^0$ mesons or a lower initial $p_T$ for both samples prior to the collisions. The $R_{AA}$ for both non-prompt and prompt $D^0$ mesons in Pb-Pb collisions aligns with the $R_{AA}$ of baryons (protons and $\Lambda$s) at low $p_T$, whereas prompt $D^0$ mesons exhibit a distinct $p_T$ dependence. These observations indicate that, at low $p_T$, hadrons and mesons derived from b-quarks are suppressed to a similar extent, while at high $p_T$, mesons from b-quarks are less suppressed than hadrons. Finally, the $R_{AA}$ for both non-prompt and prompt $D^0$ mesons in Pb-Pb collisions is consistent with the $R_{AA}$ of charm and beauty jets, which were reconstructed using jet substructure techniques. The demand for extensive millikelvin environments for quantum computing is driven by the necessity to cool numerous superconducting qubits and control lines, alongside the heat introduced by expanding system interconnects. This paper introduces a novel millikelvin platform designed to accommodate a system with up to 100 qubits, featuring a 100 W thermal margin above base temperature. Utilizing a three-stage dilution diluter, the system delivers a 1.5 L helium liquid volume at the millikelvin stage, enabling up to 100 mK through the entire distribution line. The setup includes a newly developed, compact, and robust 16-port millikelvin-grade vacuum flange, which is the first of its kind. This flange employs a compact, multi-stage, large-diameter, low-impedance design that maintains a high heat capacity, superior heat transfer, and minimal heat leak. Furthermore, the platform supports various electrical and optical measurements, including DC and RF S-parameters, DC voltage, and optical microscopy. This article details the design, construction, and performance of the large millikelvin platform at the Fermilab quantum computing testbed. The system is currently operating at approximately 7.5 mK and is scalable to 10.5 mK by integrating an additional 100 W stage. This large millikelvin platform is essential for the development of high-performance quantum computing systems. This study examines 1,045 projects utilizing 436 unique crypto implementations across seven distinct libraries to analyze common misconfigurations and potential attacks. Through a thorough investigation of these real-world libraries, we identified 107 issues, categorized into 10 distinct attack classes, and proposed specific remediation strategies for each. Our findings reveal that 71% of the problems detected are already documented in existing literature, whereas the remaining 29% represent novel vulnerabilities. Additionally, we present a framework designed to facilitate the automated identification of crypto misuses. To our knowledge, this research represents the most extensive analysis of cryptographic usage in Python projects to date. All identified issues have been submitted as new bug reports to the Python libraries involved. The source code and a web-based interface for the proposed framework are available at: https://github.com/DevSecLab/PyCryptoMisuse. Furthermore, the complete dataset of misuses can be accessed via: https://github.com/DevSecLab/PyCryptoMisuse/tree/master/PyCryptoMisuses.csv. This work is published in IEEE Access.

This paper introduces a straightforward and efficient method for automatically generating high-quality, robust urban labels. Our approach relies on a large collection of diverse urban scene segmentations. By treating this collection as a "virtual crowd," we can identify the most frequent labeling pattern across the segments, thereby extracting reliable annotations for training deep learning models. The primary advantages of automatic label generation are reduced costs and a significant reduction in the time required to create training datasets for deep learning models. The VALUE method operates without any assumptions regarding the distribution of labels within the scene or the network architecture for training deep learning models. VALUE demonstrates superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods for urban scene segmentation and object detection.
