This study examines the stability of a neutralino dark matter candidate within a $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetric framework featuring an additional Abelian gauge symmetry, U(1)$_X$. In this model, a new gauge boson Z' spontaneously breaks the U(1)$_X$ symmetry, generating a neutral neutralino as the dark matter candidate. However, Z' interactions can induce neutralino decay into a new lightest superpartner, L, via a dimension-5 effective operator mediated by a heavy scalar. The mass of the Z' boson governs the primary Z boson decay mode, while the mass of L regulates the neutralino decay, with L primarily decaying into L$\gamma$. Consequently, the dominant signature is monochromatic gamma rays originating from Z and L decays. We analyze these gamma ray signals, demonstrating that they can be distinguished from astrophysical backgrounds. Furthermore, we explore how varying the masses of the Z' and L particles influences the gamma ray spectrum and the neutralino's decay characteristics. Our findings indicate that for appropriately chosen parameters, the gamma ray spectrum exhibits two distinct peaks, offering a clear observational signature. Finally, we show that this model can account for the observed gamma ray excesses from the Galactic center and dwarf galaxies. Finally, we illustrate that by selecting suitable parameter values, the model can also explain the 130 GeV gamma ray line detected by INTEGRAL. This research underscores the significance of multi-telescope gamma-ray observations for detecting dark matter signals. Additionally, we provide projections for future gamma-ray telescopes, including the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA), the Cherenkov Telescope Array Medium Size Telescope (CTA-MST), the Wide Field Survey Telescope (SWIFT), the Cherenkov Telescope Array Large Size Telescope (CTA-LST), the European Cherenkov Telescope (E-CT), the Cherenkov Telescope (CT), and the next-generation Cherenkov Telescope (CT-NG). These projections are based on the gamma-ray spectra produced by neutralino decays. Our results suggest that advanced gamma-ray observatories will play a crucial role in dark matter detection efforts. To facilitate this, we have made our code available at \url{https://github.com/Abhishek-1234/Neutralino-DECAY.git}. We present an efficient polynomial-time approximation scheme (EPAPS) for the graph genus problem in the normal dense regime, defined as $n = \Theta(k)$ where $k$ denotes the edge count. This EPAPS surpasses the best existing approximation algorithm, achieving an error margin of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{\log k}{k})$. Our approach is grounded in a novel randomized embedding technique for normal dense graphs, which we demonstrate to be the first effective and broadly applicable method of its kind. We establish an $\mathcal{O}(\frac{\log k}{k})$ error probability for this randomized embedding, thereby enabling the EPAPS. Additionally, this result directly enhances the approximation ratio for the Zarankiewicz problem regarding nonplanar bipartite graphs. Our results are derived through the application of the Lovász Local Lemma, specifically the symmetric version formulated by Spencer. Furthermore, we introduce a new theorem concerning the chromatic number of normal dense graphs, which holds independent significance. This theorem employs the more advanced version of the Local Lemma, known as the asymmetric Lovász Local Lemma, to derive a significantly improved upper bound for the chromatic number. The proofs of both the genus approximation and chromatic number results heavily utilize the concept of "almost embeddable" graphs, which we define and analyze. We also provide a comprehensive review of the current state of research on graph genus. Finally, our work introduces a new class of random graphs, which we demonstrate possess the property of being almost embeddable with high probability. This finding offers a partial resolution to a longstanding conjecture by Bollobás and Thomason concerning the genus of random graphs. Our methodology is versatile and can be extended to address the directed version of the graph genus problem. We conclude by outlining several promising avenues for future research. Finally, our work contributes to the broader field of probabilistic combinatorics, a discipline that has been profoundly influenced by the application of the Local Lemma. We aim to advance this field by demonstrating the efficacy of the Local Lemma in solving problems within graph theory. Specifically, we illustrate how this tool can yield sharp results in extremal graph theory, a task that has previously required more cumbersome and complex arguments. Our findings thus underscore the power of the Local Lemma as a means to achieve optimal results in graph theory and contribute meaningfully to its ongoing development. We anticipate that our work will inspire further research and innovation in these areas. This paper introduces and analyzes a stochastic Newton approach designed for large-scale stochastic convex optimization. In this framework, a convex objective function is expressed as an average of $n$ individual functions, yet only a random subset of these can be accessed during each iteration. The study addresses a variant where a specific, potentially diminishing collection of functions is available at each step. The primary challenge lies in efficiently estimating the Hessian of the average function to drive the algorithm. The proposed method constructs a Hessian estimator that converges at a rate comparable to the objective function itself, thereby enabling the development of a stochastic Newton method with a provably effective iteration complexity. Notably, the proposed scheme achieves an $n$-fold reduction in complexity relative to existing deterministic first-order methods and outperforms current stochastic first-order algorithms in certain scenarios. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that the proposed method surpasses the $\mathcal{O}(n)$ complexity benchmark established for stochastic first-order methods in this context. Finally, numerical experiments are presented to validate the empirical performance of both proposals against various competitors. Keywords: Stochastic convex optimization, stochastic Newton method, stochastic coordinate descent, distributed optimization. Furthermore, we investigated transfer learning, a technique that leverages pre-trained models to enhance performance on smaller datasets. High-resolution gas time projection chambers operating in the 1-10 keVee recoil energy range serve as reactivated detectors for dark matter research, while also holding promise for neutron, nuclear, and reaccelerated medical physics applications. The superior spatial resolution of these detectors enables the calculation of energy deposition energy and location, which can be combined to form transition probability matrices. These matrices act as distinct observables for distinguishing between different recoil types. We demonstrate that such transition probability matrices offer reliable discrimination between electron and nuclear recoils for the XENON1T detector, even when utilizing only a fraction of its total light and charge data. Furthermore, we show that nuclear versus neutron recoils can be differentiated through similar methods. This approach to transition probability matrices represents a novel technique for identifying particle species and/or directions, applicable to both current and future large-scale liquid xenon experiments. Additionally, we outline a roadmap for incorporating this method into the next generation of dark matter direct detection experiments. Specifically, we demonstrate that XENONnT, with its enhanced light and charge resolution, will achieve superior nuclear/recoil performance compared to XENON1T. The transition probability matrix method is a versatile tool for reanalyzing existing data to extract physics results and for planning upcoming experiments. It offers a means to achieve the best possible nuclear recoil identification without requiring an external calibration source. Moreover, this technique can be employed to determine the direction of nuclear recoils, thereby constraining the directional signatures of dark matter and supernova neutrinos. Finally, we illustrate how this method can be adapted to constrain the angular distribution of dark matter by applying it to simulated data from a future DARWIN-like experiment. Such an approach would enable the direct measurement of dark matter directionality, offering a promising avenue for the next generation of direct detection experiments. The source code for these observables is publicly accessible at https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/TPM. Commercial driving performance evaluation is vital for ensuring road safety, yet it faces significant challenges due to the highly non-linear and contextual nature of decision-making while driving. This study introduces the concept of expert moderation, an approach where experts assess the relevance and reliability of decisions made by machine operators. We examine the effectiveness of this method through a case study involving a large transit agency, with a specific focus on how contextual factors influence decision-making. Our findings indicate that expert moderation is essential for accurately assessing decisions within commercial driving contexts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a hybrid intelligence framework, combining machine learning with expert input, offers superior performance compared to relying on either component alone. Finally, we outline the implications of this research for the broader field of intelligent decision support and future research directions. Given the extensive data availability in commercial driving, this case study holds significant potential for advancing various applications in the domain. Additionally, the intelligent framework proposed here is adaptable to other areas where decisions are highly contextual and their quality is difficult to quantify. This paper details the final outcomes of a case study designed to assess system robustness in handling words absent from the training dataset. The challenge included two distinct cases featuring extensive vocabulary domains, such as the full Wikipedia corpus (Case 1) and the complete vocabulary of the 2017 World Cup (Case 2). The participating systems spanned various categories, including neural network-based approaches, statistical methods, and hybrid neural/statistical models. Evaluation was conducted using two metrics: Mean Recall@K and Mean Recall@K+, with a total of 15 systems competing. The submission order followed this sequence: Neural+Statistical, Statistical, and finally, the neural network-based system. Ultimately, the neural+statistical model achieved the highest scores, securing first place in both cases. Second place was taken by a neural network-based system, while the pure neural model ranked third. Notably, in Case 2, the pure statistical model finished fourth. A key observation is that neural+statistical models consistently outperformed both standalone neural and statistical systems. Furthermore, the results indicate that larger models do not necessarily yield better performance. Finally, the study highlights the critical importance of vocabulary selection for OOV cases and the value of incorporating domain-specific terms. These findings offer valuable insights for enhancing system performance in scenarios involving vocabulary changes. The code can be found at: https://github.com/DeepNLP/Out-of-Vocabulary-Challenge/tree/master/Code. This work examines Gaussian random field manifolds (GRFMs) within the framework of information geometry, drawing parallels to the quotient space of free groups under inner automorphisms. We demonstrate that geodesic curves in GRFMs align with 1-parameter subgroups. Furthermore, we derive the necessary and sufficient conditions for a Lie group to be isometric with respect to the Fisher information metric, a domain that extends beyond the scope of statistical independent sources. Finally, the paper investigates the applicability of GRFMs in analyzing nontrivial statistical source models. Specifically, we establish that any multivariate time series can be represented as a GRFM by constructing an appropriate Lie group. Additionally, we show that within a specific model class, the Fisher information metric corresponds to the geodesic distance on a real form of a simple compact Lie group. The study concludes with an exploration of the geometric characteristics of the resulting data manifold. These findings are supported by numerical simulations of multivariate time series modeling and prediction. Simulation results indicate that the prediction accuracy of the proposed method surpasses that of autoregressive models, particularly in scenarios involving highly nonlinear data. Moreover, the computational complexity of this approach is significantly lower than that of other prediction techniques. As a practical application, we present the analysis of a multivariate time series derived from a simulated EEG signal. The geodesic curves associated with this EEG signal were generated using the proposed method. Additionally, we report the application of this method to a multivariate time series extracted from the M3-Data repository. Let $F$ be a cuspidal Hecke eigenform for $Sp_n(Z)$ with coefficients in a number field $K$. By applying the polylogarithm method proposed by Beilinson and Riemann method, along with the functoriality of $p$-adic integrals, we construct a $p$-adic iterated integral $J_{n,p}(t)$ defined over the pure configuration space of a specific residue $p$-adic field. We demonstrate that the denominators of the $p$-adic special values of $J_{n,p}(t)$ when evaluated at $t=1$ are bounded independently of $n$. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound for the degree of the number field required to express the Hecke eigenvalues of $F$ in $K$. Leveraging these findings, we prove that the denominators of the special values of the Langlands-Shtada $L$-functions for $F$ are bounded. Additionally, we provide a partial resolution to a conjecture by Maier, Sarnak, and Steiger regarding the boundedness of the denominators of Heike class numbers. Finally, we offer a partial answer to a conjecture by Beilinson and Levin regarding the $p$-adic regulator for the pure configuration space of a local field. This study establishes analogues of Korovkin's theorem for weakly nonlinear and monotone operators defined on Banach lattices of multivariate functions. The findings address convergence over entire domains, as well as convergence on closed subdomains characterized by multivariate side conditions or circular symmetry. Notably, the lattice structure and dimensionality are not essential; the developed analogues of Korovkin's and Nattermann's theorems apply to functions of one or more variables within standard spaces such as $C[a,b]$, $C[a,b]\times C[c,d]$, or $C[0,1]\times L^{\infty}[0,1]$. Furthermore, the results extend to closed subspaces of these spaces, including spaces of functions satisfying linear side conditions, circular symmetric functions, or satisfying the mean value property. A graph with $n$ vertices is defined as pancyclic if it contains cycles of every length from 2 to $n$. In 1972, Dirac established that any graph on $n$ vertices with a minimum degree of at least $n/2$ is both pancyclic and bipartite-pancyclic. Building upon Dirac's findings, Pajouhandeh, Schiermeyer, and Vizing recently demonstrated that for graphs with a minimum degree exceeding $2n/3 - 1$, the independence number is at most $n/3$. This paper enhances that result by proving that if the minimum degree is at least $\max\{2n/3 - 1, (n-1)^2/(2n+2)\}$, then $\alpha(G) \leq (n-1)/3$. Furthermore, we establish that if the minimum degree satisfies $\delta(G) \geq \max\{2(n-1)/3, (n-1)^2/(2n+2)\}$, the graph is pancyclic. Additionally, we show that a simple graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and a minimum degree of at least $n/2$ is pancyclic whenever its independence number is strictly less than $n/3$. Finally, we confirm that the bound $\delta(G) \geq 2(n-1)/3$ is best possible. These findings significantly extend the theorems of Pajouhandeh et al. and Dirac. Keywords: Pancyclicity; Hamiltonicity; Independence number. Mathematics Subject Classification: 05C35; 05C38. 2020. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 05C35; 05C38. 2020.

This study details the directed flow of protons, antiprotons, and pions produced in $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}=$ 200 GeV Au+Au and Xe+Xe, Xe+Au collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). Protons and antiprotons were identified using the Heavy Ion Energy Loss Detector (HIEM), whereas pion data come from the Minimum Bias Tracking System (MBTS) and Acoustic Calorimeter (AC). Protons and $\pi^-$ exhibit a negative $v_1$ in central Xe+Xe collisions that is more pronounced than the positive $v_1$ observed for pions and $\pi^+$, a pattern consistent with Au+Au and Xe+Au results. Model calculations utilizing the iEBE-VISHNU framework, which integrates the event-by-event hybrid VISHNE model with viscous hydrodynamics, align well with the experimental measurements. These findings offer new insights into the initial conditions, the system's evolution, and the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. Additionally, the ratio of directed flow for pions to that of protons shows a significantly stronger system-size dependence than the ratio of their transverse momentum spectra. This suggests that the directed flow of light hadrons is influenced by both the initial conditions and the bulk medium generated during the collision. A similar analysis of this ratio for pions and deuterons will be conducted in the near future. These results are presented as part of the collaboration's effort to disentangle the respective impacts of initial conditions and the medium on directed flow. The datasets were acquired during Run 18, the final operational period of RHIC's polarized nucleon beams. The paper concludes with a discussion of future plans for the heavy ion program. This study introduces a sparse-grid adaptive spectral Koopman (SGASK) framework designed to address dimensionality-induced computational challenges in the standard spectral Koopman method within the context of spectral element formulations. The method is built upon sparse-grid Galerkin approximations of the Koopman operator, utilizing the dual representation of the kernel to enhance computational efficiency. To further optimize performance, we develop a multilevel strategy that adaptively truncates the spectral Koopman method based on a priori error estimates derived from the dual problem. This results in the SGASK method, which offers a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost. We provide a rigorous convergence analysis for the proposed method and validate its effectiveness through various numerical experiments, including the chaotic Rössler attractor, the chaotic Lorenz attractor, and the chaotic Mackey-Glass time series. Additionally, we examine the advection equation, a one-dimensional problem featuring a highly oscillatory solution, to demonstrate the method's potential for enhancing spectral element formulations in highly oscillatory scenarios. Finally, the SGASK method is applied to predict the future states of two fluid dynamics systems: the flow around a two-dimensional airfoil and the three-dimensional jet mixing layer. In these applications, the method successfully forecasts the evolution of the lift coefficient, skin friction coefficient, and skin temperature. The method's effectiveness is confirmed by its ability to predict the long-term behavior of both the chaotic Rössler attractor and the Mackey-Glass time series. Furthermore, the method demonstrates potential for extrapolating data from high-dimensional fluid dynamics simulations, as evidenced by predictions of the three-dimensional jet mixing layer and a high-dimensional (100-dimensional) fluid dynamics simulation. All numerical experiments were conducted on a single CPU core. The SGASK method is accessible on GitHub. The exterior complex scaling (ECS) method offers a robust framework for investigating atomic and molecular systems subjected to intense direct-current (DC) fields. This approach enables the accurate calculation of non-resonant dipole polarizabilities, polarization-induced ionization rates, and resonance parameters within these atoms and molecules exposed to strong DC electric fields. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of our prior theoretical and numerical findings regarding ECS applications to atoms and molecules under such DC fields, alongside a discussion of emerging challenges and potential future research avenues. Specifically, we detail an ECS variant employing a stepwise scaling function tailored for the polarization-induced ionization of atoms and molecules. The Sinkhorn algorithm is the go-to method for solving the Schrödinger problem, yet its convergence behavior remains unclear when a solution fails to exist. This paper examines the theoretical underpinnings of that failure and presents numerical evidence regarding the algorithm's output in such cases. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Sinkhorn algorithm converges to a specific point on the boundary of the second moment space of the product of two marginals, provided this boundary point is uniquely determined by the first marginals. Furthermore, we illustrate a scenario where Sinkhorn generates an oscillating sequence, highlighting its lack of convergence in this instance. Finally, we offer a constructive illustration of how the solution to the Schrödinger problem can be derived from the algorithm's limit or oscillation when no standard solution is available. This approach is particularly valuable when the cost function is merely positive instead of being strictly positive. In these scenarios, we adapt the Sinkhorn algorithm to produce a solution, effectively demonstrating its potential for resolving cases where traditional solution existence is absent. This contribution is especially significant for applications involving Gaussian kernels, such as those found in Gaussian Process Regression. To achieve this, we provide an alternative proof for the convergence of the modified Sinkhorn algorithm when utilizing Gaussian kernels. Additionally, we offer a geometric perspective on the problem's constraints, showing that they define a convex set with a unique normal projection from the second marginals whenever these constraints are not satisfied. This insight enables the construction of a solution by relaxing the constraints. Finally, we provide a geometric interpretation of the Sinkhorn algorithm's convergence when Gaussian kernels are employed. In this context, the algorithm's limit corresponds to a geodesic projection of the second marginals onto the set defined by the problem's constraints, where the geodesics are determined by the exponential and logarithmic maps on the simplex. We also discuss the existence and uniqueness of these geodesics, noting that while they exist, they are not always unique. However, we prove that uniqueness is guaranteed when Gaussian kernels are used. These findings regarding geodesic projections and their associated geometry are of independent interest. To ensure the self-containment of this work, we have included a detailed review of relevant concepts from information geometry. Finally, we provide a comprehensive review of existing literature on the Sinkham algorithm, followed by an analysis of the specific challenges encountered when Gaussian kernels are utilized. This discussion leads to the proposal of a new Sinkham algorithm designed to address these issues. This study presents a measurement of top-quark pair ($t\bar{t}$) production in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, utilizing the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis relies on 3.00 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity collected during the LHC Run 2 period. The observed cross-section of $820.2 \pm 1.4$ (stat) $\pm 1.2$ (syst) pb aligns with standard model predictions and prior measurements conducted at lower energies. Additionally, limits are established on the production rates of third-generation vector-like quarks. The observed (expected) 95% confidence level upper bounds on the production cross-sections of color singlet and color octet vector-like quarks are 1.1 (1.4) pb and 1.1 (1.5) pb, respectively. These bounds correspond to masses of 1.1 (1.1) TeV for color singlet quarks and 1.0 (1.0) TeV for color octet quarks. Furthermore, this work introduces the first constraints on the production of a heavy charged Higgs boson ($H^\pm$) in $t\bar{t}$-associated production via the $H^\pm \to \mu^\pm \nu_\mu$ decay channel. The 95% confidence level upper limit on the production cross-section is determined to be 100 (60) fb, contingent upon the $\mu^\pm$ charge. These findings correspond to a mass of 5.02 TeV. Finally, the results also address the interpretation of a potential excess in the $\mu^+$-enriched side of the charge asymmetry. The observed (expected) 95% confidence level upper limits on the charge asymmetry are 0.03 (0.05). These constraints are consistent with measurements derived from the inclusive $t\bar{t}$-production cross-section and the forward-backward asymmetry in top-quark pair production at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV. The derived Run 2 limits on the $H^\pm$ mass are found to be 5.02 (5.02) TeV. Additionally, the study reports the first measurement of the $Z$ boson production cross-section at this energy level.

Although localized dynamics are typically restricted to non-hermitian systems or those possessing integrals of motion, we demonstrate that a system can be locally unitarily equivalent to a non-hermitian one at a specific site while remaining fully hermitian globally. The advantages of such localized properties within the Hamiltonian framework are significant for understanding and controlling dynamics. We present an explicit construction of the centramic model, a centrally non-integrable system that allows for the analytical determination of localized dynamics at a specific site. We show that the centramic model can be constructed from any pair of class $A$ random matrices, where all off-diagonal blocks vanish except for those connecting the first and last sites. The eigenstates of the centramic model are explicitly derived, and the time evolution of the first site is calculated. We find that the localized dynamics in the centramic model are governed by a single parameter, the eigenvalue associated with a special eigenstate. This parameter is determined by a competition between the coupling strength and the off-diagonal disorder of the first and last sites. We also examine the time average of the fidelity and its connection to the Poincaré recurrence time. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for a quantum search problem. This thesis aims to identify the most natural inclusion conditions for generalized Bessel functions within the Janowski class and to derive associated inequalities for their coefficients. To establish these results, we first determine the inclusion conditions for general Bessel functions in the Janowski class and subsequently derive inclusion conditions for their generalized variants. Finally, we calculate the bounds for the $n$th coefficient of Bessel functions under the Janowski class inclusion. This work represents the first study to address the inclusion conditions of generalized Bessel functions in the Janowski class and to examine the magnitude of their coefficients. The author hopes these findings will inspire further research on the inclusion properties and characteristics of generalized Bessel functions. This dissertation is divided into five chapters. The introduction will outline the background and objectives of the research. Chapter 2 will address inclusion conditions for general Bessel functions, while Chapters 3 and 4 will explore inclusion conditions for generalized Bessel functions and the magnitude of their coefficients, respectively. Given the significant role of Bessel functions in various fields, the author intends to continue researching the inclusion conditions and coefficient magnitudes for these functions in future work. Urban spaces are renowned for their social and cultural variety, yet the pandemic's behavioral shifts—specifically increased isolation and a return to home-based routines—threatened these attributes. This study quantified changes in individual and group income diversity across different urban scales using mobile phone data from Santiago, Chile. The findings indicate that income diversity declined in all settings, with the most pronounced drops occurring in residential areas and on shorter travel distances. These results highlight the potential of mobile data to measure changes in income diversity within urban encounters. Furthermore, they suggest that policies promoting interaction across home and work environments are essential for sustaining urban income diversity. The study also offers a replicable framework for analyzing income segregation and explores the broader implications of these discoveries. Finally, the research provides a method for quantifying the diversity of urban spaces, a critical step toward developing metrics for urban well-being. By grounding well-being measures in income diversity, policymakers can prioritize interventions that enhance individual opportunities and promote more equitable societies. This analysis was conducted as part of the COVID-19 Urban Challenges initiative. The code and data utilized in this study are accessible at https://github.com/urbananalytics-lab/c19-ucc-santiago. All three preconditioners are integrated into a fully-coupled nonlinear field-split framework. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the field-split nonlinear preconditioners offer superior performance compared to the author-penalty approach, with the field-split Schwarz alternating preconditioner being the most efficient of all. These findings are based on a geometric-arithmetic mean heterogeneous permeability model featuring two distinct types of channel/obstacle configurations. The research is conducted within a fully-coupled two-phase flow model utilizing a pressure formulation, solved via a fully-implicit method. Following a linearization step, a sequence of nested nonlinear problems is resolved using a sequential Schwarz alternating method. Specifically, a sequential Schwarz alternating strategy is employed for the inner nonlinear subproblems, while a Newton method is applied to the outer nonlinear problem. For the linear system arising in each outer iteration, a preconditioner is selected from three options: a locally mass-conserving Neumann Schwarz alternating method, a locally mass-conserving Dirichlet Schwarz alternating method, or a locally mass-conserving Neumann Schwarz alternating method enhanced by a locally-mass-conserving correction step. Within these nonlinear problems, a preconditioner is chosen from two variants: a field-split Schwarz alternating method using either Dirichlet or Neumann transmission conditions. Finally, for the field-split preconditioner, a specific acceleration scheme is applied to the Dirichlet variant. The performance of these preconditioners is evaluated based on the number of nonlinear iterations required to solve the pressure system. Additionally, the convergence behavior of the nested nonlinear problems is monitored through the relative $L_2$-norm of the saturation system's residual. The results indicate that the field-split preconditioner ensures both saturation and pressure convergence. We introduce an optical cavity featuring a single-handedness (chiral) structure, in which left-handed and right-handed configurations exhibit distinct resonant modes. This design is achieved by substituting half of the traditional symmetric mirror with a general complex mirror that possesses asymmetric real and imaginary components along the x-axis. Our analysis of the resonant frequency and the Pancharatnam-Berry phase demonstrates that the single-handedness of the cavity directly influences these parameters. Additionally, we show that both the real and imaginary parts of the susceptibility within the cavity material affect the resonant frequency in a handedness-dependent manner. This new cavity type is a promising design for applications in chiral quantum information processing. Furthermore, the single-handedness structure offers a potential solution to the mode-matching challenge, which is essential for achieving strong coupling between light and matter. Finally, we outline several promising avenues for future research. This study was conducted within the framework of the National Key R&D Program of China (Grant No. 2018YFB0404200). This work investigates the relationship between Jackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity and 2D gravity models, specifically focusing on the Witten model and a dilaton-dependent term in Liouville theory. We demonstrate that the JT path integral, which incorporates a negative cosmological constant $\Lambda=-\frac{1}{2\ell^2}$ on $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$, can be derived from the large-$N$ limit of a double-scaled two-dimensional non-Hermitian random matrix model. Furthermore, we show that adding Liouville theory to JT gravity corresponds to coupling the matrix model with a mass term $m$. In both frameworks, the cosmological constant is represented by $\mathbb{R}$, defined as $M=\frac{1}{\ell m}$. Additionally, we derive the path integral for JT gravity on $\mathbb{R}\times S^1$ from the matrix model and prove that incorporating Liouville theory yields the phase space associated with JT gravity on $S^2$. Finally, utilizing the matrix model, we explicitly construct the JT gravity phase space on $S^2$ when coupled with Liouville theory and discuss its connection to double-scaled 2D fermionic theories. These findings provide a systematic method for constructing JT gravity coupled with Liouville theory on $S^2$ and $\mathbb{R}\times S^1$, as well as fermionic theories on $S^2$ and $\mathbb{R}\times S^1$. Moreover, we derive the phase space for double-scaled fermionic theories from the bosonic double-scaled matrix model. As an application, we calculate the partition function for double-scaled fermionic theory on $S^2$ within the large-$N$ limit. Our results indicate that the phase space of double-scaled fermionic theory on $S^2$ is precisely JT gravity on $S^2$ coupled with Liouville theory, featuring a cosmological constant $\Lambda=-\frac{1}{2}$ and a Liouville mass $m=\frac{1}{N}$. This establishes a strong analogy between double-scaled bosonic and fermionic theories, as well as between JT gravity and Liouville theory coupled with JT gravity. We examine the matching conditions for a perfect fluid warp drive solution to Einstein's equations that include a cosmological constant. Our analysis reveals that for any non-zero cosmological constant, the warp bubble must interface with an exterior spacetime defined by a non-zero constant. In this external region, the cosmological constant assumes a distinct value compared to the interior. Specifically, when considering a non-zero constant in the exterior, the warp bubble can be filled with any equation of state provided the internal radius is sufficiently small. However, if the exterior constant is zero, the only viable filling is radiation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any warp drive solution, the null energy condition is inevitably violated. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for constructing physically realizable warp drive models. This investigation is part of a broader effort to understand the behavior of perfect fluid solutions to Einstein's equations, which is crucial for developing physically sound and realizable solutions. Ultimately, these efforts aim to establish a theoretical framework that could enable humanity to travel across the vast interstellar distances required to explore the galaxy. We introduce and implement a method to measure motional state distributions and dephasing rates of collective modes in two-dimensional ion crystals. By exciting a specific ion's spin into a superposition of ground and excited states, we couple its internal degrees of freedom to a single spatial mode. The resulting spin dephasing rate correlates with mode temperature and the second moment of the Wigner function. We validate this method by comparing its results against those from optical diagonalization. Additionally, by actively cooling the modes to near the ground state, we observe that heating rates for both diagonal and shear modes are comparable, indicating that the primary source of heating is the laser light driving the internal mode. Our approach offers a general and precise tool for diagnosing ion crystal states, which is essential for the successful implementation of large-scale quantum information processing. Furthermore, our technique is applicable to other trapped charged-particle systems, such as quantum dots. This research was conducted under an Air Force Office of Scientific Research MURI award. We introduce an ab initio time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) framework designed to investigate the tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS) mechanism. This approach models the complex TERS setup, which includes a silver substrate, a metallic AFM tip, and a molecule positioned at the tip-substrate interface. Our findings indicate that the TERS mechanism relies on two distinct components: an electromagnetic contribution, which is the conventional explanation for TERS, and a chemical effect, which is newly identified. This chemical effect stems from the molecule's ability to redistribute charge, thereby inducing a significant change in its polarizability. We demonstrate that both factors are essential for achieving the extreme signal amplification observed in TERS experiments. Furthermore, we show that both the electromagnetic and chemical effects can be quantified using the molecule's response to a strong external electric field and a intense oscillating electromagnetic wave, respectively. Finally, we establish that the probability of charge transfer between the molecule and the tip-substrate also contributes to the TERS signal. These conclusions are supported by comparing calculated spectra with experimental data. The proposed method is broadly applicable to various molecules and tip shapes, offering a versatile tool for investigating and optimizing TERS experiments. Additionally, it can be extended to other surface-enhanced vibrational spectroscopy techniques, such as SHIRS and SERS. The code is publicly accessible.11. We conducted observations of 11 nearby galaxies using the Sardinia Radio Telescope (SRT) to detect Anomalous Microwave Emission (EM). These galaxies were selected to span a wide range of star formation rates, ensuring a robust sample for statistical analysis. For the first time, we present SRT data on NGC 3077, NGC 4736, NGC 5253, NGC 5474, and NGC 6223. Additionally, we report new SRT data on M 81, M 82, M 101, UGC 1288, and UGC 9604. The observed EM flux densities align with predictions derived from star formation rates and molecular gas mass. Our results indicate that EM is detectable with the SRT in galaxies possessing star formation rates exceeding 0.1 $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, provided the molecular gas mass is at least 10% of the total interstellar gas mass. We conclude that future observations with the SRT will enable the study of EM in a larger population of nearby galaxies. Furthermore, we propose that these observations can be utilized to determine the spectral index of EM, thereby better constraining the ratio between EM and dust emission. This analysis will also help refine the understanding of EM's physical properties, such as its temperature, and the characteristics of the medium in which it occurs. Finally, the SRT's capabilities are well-suited for mapping EM in selected galaxies, which will facilitate the investigation of spatial variations in EM. The SRT's large collecting area allows for the detection of EM in galaxies at redshifts up to $z \sim 0.05$. Ammonium sulfate, a small organic molecule, exhibits an electrocaloric effect with a high entropy change, surpassing that of the largest ceramic materials. This study investigates the origins of this large entropy shift by correlating it with structural data and energy landscape characteristics. Our findings indicate that entropy is primarily stored within the energy landscape rather than the static crystal structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the high entropy density results from a combination of high entropy per unit volume and the relatively low energy of the landscape's near-degenerate states. Finally, our analysis of the entropy–temperature relationship reveals that entropy decreases linearly with rising temperature, a trait typical of electronic entropy. These insights into the source and nature of the large entropy change facilitate the design of superior functional materials. Additionally, the methodology employed to investigate the origins of entropy change can be applied to other systems, such as phase transitions in InGaAs. Although numerous studies have demonstrated the existence of neural systems utilizing optimal strategies, such as the dopamine midbrain encoding reward prediction errors, the extent to which humans employ these mechanisms in everyday decision-making remains unclear. This study investigates the behavioral and neural characteristics associated with the deployment of near-optimal strategies. We utilized a computational approach to categorize behavioral data from a decision-making task into a spectrum of strategies, ranging from optimal to those governed by simple heuristic rules. Our results indicate that, on average, participants exhibited a moderate degree of optimization, with optimization levels remaining stable over time and demonstrating low inter-individual variability. Furthermore, individual differences in optimization levels correlated with variations in the midbrain's prediction error signal. These findings suggest a potential mechanism explaining why some individuals may be more susceptible to cognitive biases than others. Finally, we offer a discussion of the broader implications of these results for understanding the function of neural systems. This study addresses the Approximate Near Neighbor Search (ANNN) problem under the Fréchet distance metric. Given a dataset $\mathcal{P}$ of $n$ polygonal curves in a $d$-dimensional Euclidean space, a query set $\mathcal{Q}$ of $m$ such curves, an error tolerance $\varepsilon > 0$, and a multiplicative factor $\tau \geq 1$, the objective is to design a data structure for $\mathcal{P}$ that, upon receiving a query curve $q \in \mathcal{Q}$, returns a point $p \in \mathcal{P}$ satisfying $\text{opt}(p, q) \leq \tau \cdot \text{opt}(p', q)$ for all $p' \in \mathcal{P}$, where $\text{opt}(p', q)$ represents the optimal Fréchet distance between $p'$ and $q$. We establish a data structure with a space complexity of $O(d^2\log^{O(1)}n)$ and a query complexity of $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n \cdot m \cdot \text{polylog}(m))$ that identifies a point $p \in \mathcal{P}$ with a diameter at most $2\cdot \text{opt}(p, q)$ relative to $q$, thereby solving the ANNN problem with $\tau = 2$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach is nearly optimal by proving that any data structure achieving the specified space and query complexities must address the ANNN problem with $\tau = \Omega(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$. Additionally, we present a method utilizing $O(d\log^{O(1)}n)$ space and $O(m \cdot \text{polylog}(m))$ query time to solve the problem in the $L_\infty$ metric with $\tau = 2$. Finally, we introduce a combinatorial algorithm with runtime $O(n\log^{O(1)}n \cdot m \cdot \text{polylog}(m))$ that computes the optimal Fréchet distance between two polygonal curves, improving upon the previous best runtime by a factor of $n$. Our primary contributions are the first algorithms to simultaneously achieve both optimal space and query complexities for the ANNN problem under the Fréchet distance. This study introduces a straightforward yet potent approach to model mitigation for this type of error. The method relies on iterative Bayesian unfolding, which utilizes a machine learning framework to refine predictions regarding the true data-generating distribution. We evaluate the technique across various mitigation scenarios and demonstrate that it surpasses baseline methods, particularly when dealing with coarse error distributions. This paper tackles the challenge of teaching a robot to understand and execute new instructions from a human teacher. The robot relies on a set of conventions that map human behaviors to specific actions; however, these conventions often remain implicit, meaning a robot may fail to grasp them without explicit guidance. This study addresses how a teacher can communicate these conventions to a robot and demonstrates that shared autonomy serves as an effective method for this transfer of knowledge. In this approach, the teacher programs the robot's behavior while the robot retains control over aspects of the task. We validate this approach across two domains: a physical simulation involving a Khepera III robot navigating a maze, and a virtual environment where a human plays a video game alongside a robot to teach game-specific rules. Our results indicate that shared autonomy successfully communicates conventions to the robot, enabling it to execute tasks that were previously unachievable. Furthermore, simulation data reveals that this method is sample-efficient, allowing the robot to learn effectively from a limited number of experiences. Finally, a user study confirms that human observers perceive this teaching approach as effective. Overall, the paper establishes that shared autonomy is a viable and practical technique for conveying implicit conventions to robots. This technique is particularly advantageous when a task requires a sequence of behaviors where the robot must identify when to apply each convention based on contextual cues. The code and simulation files are publicly available at https://github.com/alexisbostrom/shared-autonomy-conventions. Supplementary materials, including details from the user study, can be found in the supplementary section. Our key contributions are: (1) a novel teaching method that leverages shared autonomy to communicate conventions, (2) an evaluation across diverse domains demonstrating the method's effectiveness, (3) an assessment of human perceptions regarding the value of shared autonomy in convention teaching, and (4) open-source code supporting these contributions. Our findings are as follows: (1) the shared autonomy method is effective in both physical and digital settings, (2) robots utilizing this method can generalize to new tasks, and (3) humans regard the shared autonomy approach as a valuable way to instruct robots. We introduce HiTMap, a novel hierarchical topological map designed for navigation in unseen environments. This representation combines the scalability of hierarchical planning with the graph-based resilience to occlusions found in topological maps, while additionally offering absolute loop closure and relative pose estimates between nodes. The hierarchical structure facilitates efficient path computation, whereas the topology allows for occlusion-tolerant navigation in unknown settings. Furthermore, the map's connectivity and relative geometry enable survival in environments with significant loop closures. We demonstrate HiTMap's effectiveness across three benchmark datasets and validate its success through simulation and physical experiments. The corresponding source code is available at https://github.com/hiit-lab/HiTMap.

To meet the growing demands of wireless communication systems, we introduce two new multivariable-based approaches for generating two-dimensional (2-D) Z-complementary array code sets. The first method employs multivariable functions to map one-dimensional (1-D) inter-group complementary code sets (1-D-ICCS) into 1-D Z-complementary sequences, which are then arranged into 2-D Z-complementary array code sets. The second method utilizes multivariable functions to map 1-D-ICCS into 2-D Z-complementary array code sets directly. Both methods support flexible parameter selection, allowing for an adjustable ratio between the peak-to-mean power ratio (PMPR) and the maximum correlation. Numerical simulations confirm the validity of these two approaches. Notably, the second method offers significant advantages in terms of 2-D array structure design flexibility and computational efficiency. These results demonstrate the feasibility of constructing 2-D Z-complementary array code sets, thereby expanding the application potential of these codes in wireless communication systems. Additionally, the proposed methods can be extended to other types of Z-complementary array code sets. A MATLAB-based algorithm for generating these codes is also provided. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/zhongyuanwang1989/Z-complementary-code-set-generator. This study investigates how electron spill-out and nonlocality influence light propagation within the gap separating two metallic surfaces. By analyzing solutions to the boundary-integral equation for this confined region, we demonstrate that these quantum effects substantially alter plasmonic modes and the associated electromagnetic energy density as the gap size approaches zero. Specifically, we show that gap-plasmons do not necessarily converge to the single-metal plasmons of the zero-gap limit; instead, their existence and characteristics depend on the rate at which the gap closes. These findings underscore the critical role of quantum phenomena in the physics of plasmons in ultrasmall gaps and suggest new avenues for achieving highly nonlocal light-matter interactions in the nanometer scale. Finally, our results are validated using experimental data and by comparing them with solutions to the quantum-hydrodynamic equations. Additionally, we identify a novel regime of nonlocal surface modes that emerge when the gap is separated by a dielectric material. These modes exhibit long wavelengths and weak coupling to the metallic surfaces, making them potentially detectable in optical experiments. We also highlight the distinct characteristics of these nonlocal surface modes compared to traditional plasmons. The methodologies developed in this work offer a versatile framework for exploring the influence of quantum effects on light propagation in nanoscale systems. Furthermore, we provide an open-source Python package, PyGapPlasmons, which implements these methods and can be utilized for such investigations. PyGapPlasmons is accessible at https://github.com/PyGapPlasmons. The source code for all calculations presented in this study is available at https://github.com/PyGapPlasmons/gap-plasmons-examples. We introduce a new framework designed to facilitate interactive exploration of multivariate time series and longitudinal data by leveraging temporal context and allowing data to be manipulated across the time axis. This method employs time-based direct manipulations, such as sliding, to enhance data exploration. The paper details the design and implementation of these time-based sliding interactions, supported by a methodological design process, a methodological description, and a case study. The richness of information within Electronic Health Records (EHRs) offers significant potential for uncovering critical disease insights. However, current methods struggle to effectively leverage the heterogeneous nature of EHR data, which comprises diverse clinical entities like diagnoses, medications, and symptoms. This paper introduces the Heterogeneous Similarity Graph Neural Network (HSGNN), a novel approach designed to extract meaningful patterns from EHR data. We construct a heterogeneous EHR graph where both entities and relations are modeled as nodes, and similarity is integrated into the edge weights. To capture global structural patterns, we employ a multi-hop graph attention mechanism. Furthermore, a node-level attention layer is implemented to concentrate on local features, while a node activation mechanism enhances the representation of sparsely connected nodes. The efficacy of HSGNN is validated through a diabetes prediction task. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the model's robustness and interpretability. Our results demonstrate that HSGNN outperforms several baseline models in prediction accuracy and exhibits robustness against noise. Finally, the model generates interpretable explanations that highlight the most influential entities and relationships within an individual's EHR. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1993/HSGNN. **Index Terms:** Heterogeneous Similarity Graph Neural Network, Electronic Health Records, Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network, Predictive Analysis.

Automated requirement extraction is a critical challenge in software engineering, yet it is difficult due to the disorganized nature of source materials like design documents, emails, and issue reports. This study investigates the feasibility of automatically deriving requirements from such unstructured resources. We constructed a new corpus featuring issue requests and designs from two software engineering projects, annotated to identify sentences that yield issues or designs. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that: (1) a single annotator can achieve a reasonable extraction rate; (2) machine learning models can extract requirements from unstructured text with a reasonable degree of accuracy; and (3) the quality of extracted requirements is high, as most can be mapped to established requirement types or combined into new ones. Consequently, our empirical evidence suggests that machine learning-based requirement extraction is a viable approach for software engineering applications. Furthermore, we outline the potential utility of this method in issue management and specification engineering, while also addressing current limitations and proposing directions for future research. Finally, we discuss how such extraction techniques could inform adaptive software engineering practices. We introduce a fully relativistic, first-principles theory designed to calculate the spectral properties of localized Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states. This theory is applied to an Mn adatom and an Mn dimer situated on an Nb(110) surface. Our findings indicate that spin-orbit coupling (SOC) is essential for accurately reproducing the finite gap in the local density of states (LDOS) near the Fermi level, as well as for determining the correct sign of the YSR-state splitting in the case of Mn dimers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that YSR states can be observed in tunneling experiments involving two Mn dimers on Nb(110) when the tip is positioned above the dimer. Additionally, SOC is required to replicate the experimentally observed antiferromagnetic ordering of the dimers. Finally, we show that the magnetic anisotropy of the yolk-like dimers is primarily driven by SOC. These results provide a comprehensive theoretical basis for interpreting recent tunneling spectroscopy studies on Mn dimers on Nb(110) and suggest that the observed magnetic anisotropy of the dimers can be attributed to the local exchange coupling between the atoms. Our results also suggest that YSR states could be realized in other dimers on Nb(110) that exhibit a pronounced magnetic anisotropy. This could be achieved by selecting dimers with a specific symmetry axis aligned along a high-symmetry direction of the Nb(110) surface. In such cases, the YSR states would be split by spin-orbit interactions, resulting in tunneling conductance peaks that are asymmetric with respect to the chemical potential. This provides a clear explanation for the recently reported asymmetric conductance peaks for the yolk-like dimers. Overall, our results suggest that the unique properties of the yolk-like dimers are due to the local exchange coupling between the dimers. Distribution-to-distribution (D2D) registration is a critical operation in the 3D vision pipeline, which serves as the foundation for numerous applications. However, the bias inherent in D2D registration can lead to inaccurate results. While distribution-based methods have been developed to mitigate this issue, they often suffer from high computational costs and are sensitive to noise. This paper introduces a distribution-based filter utilizing deep neural networks to reduce bias in D2D registration. Our method operates without requiring corresponding point pairs, making it suitable for noisy and unorganized point clouds. We demonstrate the filter's effectiveness through a 3D object recognition task, where it achieves superior performance compared to both traditional optimization-based and existing distribution-based techniques. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/3dv-ai/D2D-DNN. Additionally, the method is integrated into the open-source 3D vision library OpenNNA. Our results confirm that the proposed D2D-DNN filter is computationally efficient, capable of processing point clouds of various sizes in under 10 milliseconds. The method is also available in the popular PointNet library. Furthermore, we provide a Python implementation of a simple usage example for easy experimentation. We hope this work inspires future research on distribution-based techniques for 3D vision challenges. The Python code can be found at https://github.com/3dv-ai/D2D-DNN. Satellite imagery is frequently employed to identify the boundaries of natural features, including forests, rivers, and roads. While deep learning methods have achieved significant advancements in the recent decade, edge detection remains a persistent challenge in image processing. This study introduces a non-local deep image prior that outperforms Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and traditional approaches like Canny and RoF. Furthermore, the proposed model offers the flexibility to automatically adjust hyperparameters based on specific image characteristics. Experimental results demonstrate that the method produces high-quality outputs even with limited training data. The model's parameters are optimized via a non-local term utilizing Quadratic Total Variation (QTV) regularization and a discriminator trained through an adversarial framework. Notably, the discriminator functions as a pre-trained feature extractor that can be reused across different datasets. The approach was evaluated on the ISPRS Vaihingen and Potsdam satellite image datasets, with comparisons against CNN-based techniques and classical edge detection algorithms. The paper includes comparative analysis and visual examples of detected edges. The results indicate that the proposed model effectively identifies edges for diverse natural objects, such as roads, rivers, and forests. Additionally, the study explores applications in segmenting these objects using an image prior framework. The proposed framework is implemented in PyTorch and is available at: https://github.com/ashishkumar1998/Non-local-DEP. Future research will focus on enhancing performance through more robust hyperparameter optimization techniques. Finally, the model demonstrates promising applications for object detection and classification. Keywords: Edge Detection, Deep Image Prior, Quadratic Total Variation Regularization, Adversarial Training, Segmentation.

We introduce a new approach to modeling time-resolved X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) data, specifically for samples subjected to intense, ultrafast X-ray pulses. This modeling technique incorporates a non-linear, fluence-dependent electron emission rate, enabling a direct quantification of the electron yield relative to incident photon flux. By utilizing this method, researchers can compare electron production across different fluences and compare samples under identical conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the model's utility in analyzing time-resolved XANES data from liquid water, offering a straightforward explanation for observed discrepancies between experimental results and standard theoretical simulations. This study represents the first application of rate equations to XANES modeling. We anticipate that fluence-dependent electron emission is a universal phenomenon in hard X-ray spectroscopy, particularly at high intensities, thereby making this modeling framework broadly applicable. Additionally, we outline a strategic plan for developing an enhanced water model to facilitate future comparisons between theory and experiment. Finally, we propose that this methodology is well-suited for future applications in time-resolved XANES experiments involving semiconductor materials. In such contexts, electron emission can be leveraged to measure electron-hole pair generation rates, offering a new avenue for investigating ultrafast electron dynamics in semiconductors. These advances are expected to significantly impact the design and interpretation of experiments within the upcoming LCLS-II hard X-ray scientific program. Deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, which involve adding carefully engineered perturbations to input signals that humans cannot perceive. These attacks exploit the fact that digital representations of analog waveforms in the real world are discrete, leading to digital-specific adversarial examples that cause DNNs to produce incorrect classifications. This study introduces a novel resiliency technique that enhances robustness against such attacks. The approach employs a generative adversarial network (GAN) to synthesize a mixture of multiple modulation schemes, creating a diverse training dataset. By training the digital communication classifier on this varied mixture, the model's resilience is improved. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed GAN-generated mixture dataset achieves an average robustness gain of 1.5% against adversarial attacks. Furthermore, the method maintains accuracy comparable to non-adversarial datasets on clean data. The source code for the resiliency framework is available at https://github.com/raja-singh-1/GAN-Resiliency. The simulations were conducted using the open-source Starlink Software Defined Radio Framework, which models the complete Starlink signal chain. Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neurological condition characterized by demyelination within the central nervous system. MS lesions, which appear as hyperintense areas on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, are essential for diagnosing the disease. However, manual segmentation of these lesions is time-consuming and demands specialized expertise. Deep learning has emerged as a viable alternative, yet it typically requires extensive training data. This study investigates the segmentation of MS lesions using models trained and fine-tuned on data from four hospitals, comparing two strategies: \textit{I.} continual training and fine-tuning across all hospitals, and \text{II.} training and fine-tuning on a subset of three hospitals while excluding one. The goal is to assess whether model performance degrades when the top-performing hospital is omitted from the training set. The findings indicate that both approaches yield comparable results, with no significant drop in performance when excluding the best-performing hospital. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that a base model can be developed and continually fine-tuned across all hospitals using just a few scans per institution, achieving state-of-the-art performance. This is particularly significant given the scarcity of annotated MS lesions in most hospitals. The code and models are accessible at \url{https://github.com/DeepBrainTechnologies/Datasets-and-Methods-MS-Lesion-Segmentation}. This work is part of the Multiple Sclerosis Datasets and Methods Challenge organized by DeepBrain Technologies at MICCAI 2021. Participants may access the data and models via the challenge's submission portal at \url{https://dmt-multiple-sclerosis-challenge.github.io/submit/}. We introduce a novel metric comparison, analogous to Alexandrov's, and demonstrate its significant link to the continuity of optimal transport for regular measures on Riemannian manifolds, especially concerning the MTW condition formulated by Ma, Trudinger, and Wang. Furthermore, we apply this comparison to establish the regularity of optimal transport maps within the small MTW condition framework, closely aligned with the conditions established by Loeper and Gangbo and Lacey. Finally, we examine the specific case of comparison tensors, which are more accessible to explicit calculation than the Loci curvature tensor. These tensors have previously aided in proving the Alexandrov curvature of comparison metrics in Euclidean and Hilbertian settings, as well as in deriving necessary and sufficient conditions for the continuity of optimal transport maps in those contexts. Our work offers an alternative necessary and sufficient condition for the continuity of optimal transport maps based on the comparison tensor, thereby generalizing existing curvature conditions found in the literature. Additionally, we provide an explicit formula for these tensors in terms of the metric, connection, and Hessian. As an application, we utilize this formula to verify the comparison condition for a specific class of Finsler metrics, including those arising from the squared distance function on Euclidean spaces with obstacles. This result confirms the regularity of optimal transport maps associated with such metrics. The methodology for this verification draws inspiration from the approach used by Gangbo and Lacey. Finally, we illustrate the utility of comparison tensors by examining the necessary and sufficient conditions for the continuity of optimal transport maps in the context of Finsler geometry. This condition relies on a newly defined class of tensors, the Comparison Gradient Hessian (CGH) tensor, which offers a more tractable alternative to the Comparison Loci curvature tensor. Notably, the necessity of this condition is established without assuming the convexity of the Finsler metric. The paper concludes with several illustrative examples. This condition represents a significant generalization of the small MTW condition, the pinching condition, and the nonFinslerized necessary condition for the convexity of the distance function. Furthermore, it provides a necessary condition for the convexity of the distance function within the broader context of Finsler geometry. Dynamical systems are increasingly utilized to represent complex phenomena across physics, engineering, and the social sciences. These models are typically parameterized and rely on numerical methods for solution, necessitating rigorous error analysis. However, achieving accurate predictions from dynamical systems is complicated by two primary issues: inherent model errors and numerical discretization errors. This study introduces a machine learning framework designed to learn and correct model errors in dynamical systems. We demonstrate the application of this approach to improve the accuracy of the Lorenz and Van der Pol models. Furthermore, we evaluate the framework's ability to learn errors in systems where analytical error terms are known, providing insights into its potential for use in high-dimensional and data-driven models. Our proposed method offers a pathway for integrating machine learning into dynamical system modeling and could enhance the accuracy of various applications, including weather forecasting and fluid flow prediction. We present high-resolution (0.02 pc) dust continuum observations of the Dragon infrared dark cloud, specifically targeting the newly identified dense core candidate, G030.3+00.3 (G030). This core is situated within the 10 K column density map of G030 and aligns with the site of the 24 $\mu$m source G030.3+00.3N. By analyzing dust emission data across 1.3, 2.0, 3.0, and 4.8 mm wavelengths, we derived dust temperatures and spectral indices for the G030 core. These spectral indices reveal a transition from a flatter value of 2.0 at sub-millimeter wavelengths to a steeper value of 3.0 at millimeter wavelengths. This shift suggests a core growth mechanism where smaller dust grains accumulate in the cold outer envelope, while larger grains settle toward the core's center. The G030 core exhibits a compact size of 0.02 pc and a mass of 1000 M$_\odot$, with a mass spectral index of 2.5. These characteristics indicate that G030 is a dense core in the early stages of collapse, with its structure consistent with the core growth model proposed by Henning et al. (2010). Furthermore, the G030 core is likely in the process of forming a massive star. The spectral energy distribution of the G030.3+00.3N source is best modeled by a 1000 K blackbody, which aligns with the temperature of the dust surrounding a massive protostar. Additionally, the spectral index of this source is 2.0, matching the value observed in the inner region of the G030 core. These findings support the hypothesis that the G030.3+00.3N source is a massive protostar currently forming within the G030 core. Finally, the G030 core represents a critical component of the Dragon molecular cloud, serving as a vital link in the core growth model that explains how massive stars form in the cloud's densest regions. This study is the first to provide evidence of core growth in the Dragon cloud, a phenomenon that was previously unobserved. Primordial black holes (PBHs) are a promising dark matter candidate, with specific mass ranges previously highlighted by observational constraints. However, the formation dynamics of PBHs and their influence on the early universe remain poorly understood. This study employs PopSyCLE, a new code designed to simulate PBH formation and evolution, to investigate how different formation scenarios affect astrophysical constraints. We analyze two specific models: (1) the collapse of overdensities within a radiation-dominated fluid, and (2) the collapse of overdensities in a radiation-dominated fluid containing a primordial black hole seed. Our findings indicate that, depending on the underlying formation model, the PBH density can be approximately 10% of the total matter density. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the presence of a seed mass can alter the density profile, causing overdensities to collapse into a single PBH with a significantly higher final mass. Finally, we show that the astrophysical constraints on the PBH fraction vary by several orders of magnitude, contingent on both the formation model and the specific constraints being examined. This research underscores the necessity of incorporating formation models when investigating PBHs as dark matter candidates. For a system width (corresponding to the wedge height) normalized to the sphere diameter of $L_d=2.25$, a phase transition from a disordered state to a locally ordered state featuring splay modulation was observed as density increased. The characteristics of the resulting splay-modulated phase closely resemble those found in systems of hard bilobes and bispheres, despite the fundamental difference in wedge geometry: the ball-based wedge model allows wedges to interact along their entire length, whereas the bilobes and bispheres models restrict interaction to the region corresponding to the wedge head. The system exhibits a phase diagram with two distinct locally ordered phases—a splay-modulated phase and a shear-modulated phase with compression modulation—and a first-order transition line connecting the endpoints of these coexisting regions. The boundaries of the splay- and shear-modulated phases display strong similarities to those in systems of hard bilobes and bispheres. Furthermore, we identified a coexistence region between a crystal and a liquid, which aligns with previous findings in this system. The phase boundaries between locally ordered states and between ordered and disordered states in this study are consistent with those reported for systems utilizing continuous geometric approximations of wedges based on circular arcs. Finally, we demonstrated that the transition between locally ordered states in this system is first-order, contrasting with the second-order transition observed in systems of hard bilobes. These findings suggest that the interaction range along the wedge axis is a critical factor in determining the nature of the transition between locally ordered states. Parameter-efficient methods have recently gained significant attention for pre-trained language model adaptation. This study introduces a straightforward yet effective framework that adjusts only the representations of special tokens. Our approach involves injecting one or more novel tokens into the existing token vocabulary, initializing and training their parameters via fine-tuning, while keeping the original token representations fixed. When these parameters are frozen, the pre-trained language model functions as a robust textual feature extractor. We evaluate our method on three standard classification benchmarks, demonstrating that it rivals or surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, we expand upon the method's capabilities by applying it to graph node classification and image recognition tasks. On these visual and structural datasets, our approach not only outperforms leading baseline models but also exceeds the results of recent promising proposals. The code is accessible at https://github.com/robinage/STAP. Finally, we highlight the method's versatility by utilizing it for natural language inference and machine translation. In these scenarios, our technique generates high-quality outputs that are indistinguishable from those produced by more complex alternatives. Overall, this research underscores the method's capacity to deliver state-of-the-art performance across a diverse spectrum of domains. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.01651. Keywords: Pre-trained Language Model Tuning, Special Tokens, Graph Neural Networks, Computer Vision.

This paper investigates the preference addition of independent sets, introducing a non-contextual model grounded in the joint probability distribution of the four bivariate random sets formed by the pairwise combinations of the two input bipartite random sets. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for this distribution to serve as a consistent preference relation across the independent set pairs. The addition operation is executed through the Stochastic Dominance of the sum of these random sets. Furthermore, we contrast this non-contextual approach with two established contextual models for preference addition. Numerical examples illustrate the distinctions among the three methods, and simulation studies evaluate their relative performance. Our findings indicate that the non-contextual model's advantage lies in its simplicity, eliminating the need to estimate a joint multivariate distribution. However, its limitations include higher computational costs and, in certain scenarios, a reduced ability to express preference between the resulting independent sets compared to the contextual models. Ultimately, the choice among these models should be guided by the specific characteristics of the problem at hand. This research paves the way for developing new non-contextual models for preference addition. Consequently, a primary contribution is a set of necessary and sufficient conditions for the consistency of a non-contextual preference addition model, a contribution that is both novel and valuable. Additionally, the simulation study offers valuable insights for future work aiming to design non-contextual models for preference addition. Notably, the consistency conditions for the non-contextual model are less restrictive than those required by the contextual models. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews foundational concepts and existing models for preference set addition. Section 3 proposes the non-contextual model and derives its consistency conditions, which are more permissive than those of contextual models. Section 4 compares the three models using both analytical and numerical approaches. Finally, Section 5 concludes the study and outlines directions for future research. The originality of this work stems from the development of the non-contextual addition model, the derivation of its consistency conditions, the comprehensive comparison among the three models, and the assessment of their performance through simulation studies. These contributions are essential for advancing the theory of preference set addition. The originality and novelty of this research are significant, and the comparison of these models is a crucial contribution. The paper is original, and no part of it has been previously published. This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant Nos. 71701024 and 71571025). The corresponding author is Prof. Xiaoguang Mei.

This study examines the thermodynamic and dynamic interdependencies among various free-volume and thermodynamic fragility metrics in a glass-forming polymer near its glass transition. We establish a quantitative relationship between these parameters and their associated activation energies. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that a simple mode-coupling theory framework successfully captures the links between thermodynamic and dynamic characteristics in these supercooled fluids. Finally, we discuss the applicability of these results to other glass-forming materials. A key contribution of our work is the revelation that the thermodynamic and dynamic properties of these complex fluids are not independent; rather, they are tightly coupled through the activation energies governing structural relaxation. This insight may facilitate the development of a comprehensive theory that unifies thermodynamic and dynamic properties, a goal that remains elusive for many glass-forming systems. The data and analysis used to support these conclusions are available at https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.macromol.0c02207.
