This study investigates the Soret effect arising from the internal degrees of freedom of soft molecular solutes. Using a two-temperature molecular dynamics framework, we demonstrate that thermal excitation of these internal modes during temperature gradients generates an additional current component linked to internal energy. This new contribution enhances the primary mass current driven by the gradient, thereby amplifying the enhanced diffusion coefficient, $D_T/D$, which quantifies the Soret effect. The framework is validated by comparing simulation results with experimental data for polyethylene glycol (PEG) and benzene. We conclude that internal degrees of freedom in soft molecules play a significant role in determining the Soret effect under temperature gradients. These findings are pertinent to the separation of organic compounds via membrane filtration and the separation of isotopes using gas diffusion. Furthermore, the theoretical approach is applicable to analyzing the mass current induced by temperature gradients in systems exhibiting size asymmetry, internal degree of freedom asymmetry, and charge asymmetry. Finally, we outline potential future research directions concerning the cross-effects induced by internal degrees of freedom under external fluxes. \textit{(Keywords: Soret effect, internal degrees of freedom, soft molecules, separation, cross-effects)} \textit{(Published in \textit{Phys. Low-quality music recordings, often captured by consumer devices like smartphones, frequently suffer from distortions such as background noise, reverberation, and microphone-induced frequency biases. This study introduces a deep learning framework to simulate the characteristics of a high-fidelity audio system for music enhancement. Unlike traditional methods, our approach does not require knowledge of the specific system parameters. Instead, a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) learns to model a hypothetical high-quality audio system by translating music stems from a low-fidelity representation to a high-fidelity one. To evaluate the acoustic quality of the generated signals, we employ an encodation function that converts audio into a latent space designed to capture musical attributes. Finally, an iterative optimization process is utilized to train the network. Experiments conducted on the MusiQA dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of this method. Additionally, we incorporate music vocalization, an underexplored task, to further validate our approach. Both qualitative and quantitative results confirm the success of our proposed framework. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/music-enhancement-v2. In summary, this work presents a novel method for music enhancement. Our contributions are threefold: (1) we propose a new music enhancement framework utilizing a cGAN and an audio-to-image translation function; (2) we introduce a new music quality assessment dataset, which represents the first such dataset in this domain; and (3) we demonstrate the application of StyleGAN music vocalization for the first time. The results indicate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in music enhancement. Our work is expected to inspire further research into audio distortion removal and sound quality assessment. The dataset can be accessed at: https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/MusicEnhancement. This paper introduces a new dataset designed to investigate the consequences of a sudden release of force during object throwing. We examine three distinct scenarios: releasing the object too early, too late, or too soon after grip initiation. Our findings indicate that while releasing too early causes the object to fall short, releasing too late still results in an undershoot, albeit over a longer trajectory. Additionally, we observed that increasing the duration between grip initiation and release significantly raises the forces applied to the object. These insights are achieved without any prior information about the specific experimental conditions. We trained a policy using our newly introduced condition-agnostic training approach and validated its efficacy through both simulation and physical robot experiments. This methodology offers a straightforward and effective way to generate diverse data for complex throwing tasks. Furthermore, the experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach enables a generalized throwing policy that is robust to variations in the point of release. The dataset and accompanying code will be made available at https://github.com/leeyang123/FauxThrow. Finally, we hope this work inspires further research into throwing dynamics and facilitates a more comprehensive understanding of the forces involved in throwing objects. The term "FauxThrow" is derived from the French word "faux," meaning "incorrect" or "false," reflecting the study's focus on the impact of an incorrect release point. We believe this perspective will foster a broader appreciation of the forces at play in throwing activities. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) relies on beam decoding to balance the encoder-decoder interface with fluency and accuracy. However, this process lacks an explicit mechanism to manage the fluency-autonomy trade-off within the decoder, leading to suboptimal translations. Furthermore, current beam-search decoders fail to leverage linguistic knowledge from NMT's multilingual pre-training. To address these issues, we introduce a tree-structured decoding approach that integrates syntactic connections into the search space. This method utilizes the parse tree generated during the NMT pre-training phase to define a top-down decoding tree, which is then merged with the neural search tree. By integrating this top-down tree search space with a dynamic syntactic connections strategy, the decoder can effectively regulate the fluency-autonomy trade-off while incorporating rich linguistic knowledge. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances translation quality. Additionally, we apply this method to unconstrained dependency parsing, achieving a substantial improvement in unlabeled attachment score (UAS). Finally, an ablation study confirms that our method improves the general sequence-to-tree decoding performance. The binding energy (BE) of molecules on icy grains is a critical parameter for modeling astrochemical reactions on interstellar dust. This value significantly influences radical formation, which in turn affects accretion rates and reaction barriers. However, the diverse origins of BE data in current literature—ranging from experimental measurements to various computational methods—often make it difficult to assess reliability or convert between scales. To address this, we introduce the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP), a database containing BEEPs (Binding Energy Evaluation Packages) for small molecules. These packages compile BE values from multiple literature sources, enabling users to correlate and convert the data. Additionally, BEEP includes a comprehensive review of BE calculation methods and a newly developed, efficient protocol for deriving accurate BEs. The platform is accessible at http://beep.astroscu.sc.edu. We anticipate that BEEP will serve as a valuable resource for astrochemists, facilitating the design of more accurate models for astrochemical reactions. We will continue to expand the database to include additional molecular species. The study examines a multiplicative stochastic process constrained by a lognormal lower bound. A model for this process is developed, deriving its distribution function—which relies on four parameters—and associated statistical characteristics. By calibrating the parameters, the analysis demonstrates that the theoretical distribution aligns with empirical distributions observed in specific real-world datasets. Furthermore, the paper explores potential applications for this distribution, illustrating its utility through various examples. Notably, the study highlights its suitability for analyzing phenomena involving sizes, durations, or other positive-valued metrics that exhibit power-law statistics. Additionally, the distribution is recommended for applications requiring a lower tail that approaches linearity on a log-log plot. A comparative analysis of several real datasets confirms that the fitted distribution often outperforms the lognormal distribution. Finally, the paper introduces a variant of Benford's law designed for these types of distributions. The law is derived, and numerical validation is provided through comparisons with other distribution types. The results indicate that while this variant of Benford's law is not universal, it holds significant potential for applications in data forensics. A novel metric called the "Benford distance" is proposed for this purpose, with numerical examples demonstrating its effectiveness. The paper concludes by outlining the limitations of this forensics approach. The source code is available at https://github.com/alejo117/benford-law-for-multiplicative-stochastic-processes. Alejo117. We present a new approach for estimating expectations of observables, designed to mitigate the critical challenge of requiring extensive sampling from deeply nested nested commutators. Our method achieves a total classical postprocessing complexity that scales polynomially with the number of qubits, order of noise, and desired precision, while utilizing $N_{\text{exp}}$ shots from shallow circuits of depth $N_{\text{exp}}^{1/3}$. This represents a substantial improvement over prior techniques, such as the original shadow protocol, which demands depth proportional to the noise order. We validate the efficacy of our proposed "shadow shadow" through tests on various observables, including Pauli operators, nested commutators, and the Hamiltonian of the 2D transverse-field Ising model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method surpasses alternative recent strategies, including network compression and nested commutator measurement, by necessitating fewer distinct circuit configurations. Finally, we illustrate the method's utility in two applications: characterizing the non-unitary dynamics induced by noise and inferring noise characteristics from experimentally accessible data. These examples underscore that our approach is both practical and highly effective. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Quantinuum/shadow-shadow. By applying a specific limiting procedure, the large $|k|$ asymptotics for DSI II are derived from the general case. Additionally, it is noted that the direct scattering data for DSI II is equivalent to that of DSI I, differing only by a constant multiplicative factor. Meta-learning seeks to create models capable of rapidly adapting to new environments using only a few examples. This paper investigates meta-learning within the framework of online linear regression, where an algorithm must dynamically adjust to unknown, time-varying sub-Gaussian distributions. The objective is to achieve low cumulative regret relative to the best static linear model selected in hindsight. We introduce an efficient meta-algorithm that provably learns a linear representation from data, demonstrating that cumulative regret against the optimal static model is logarithmic with high probability. Furthermore, we present a straightforward analysis of our algorithm's performance, showing it attains a polylogarithmic regret bound in the sample size. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to evaluate the practical efficacy of our proposed method. Our results indicate that meta-algorithms are competitive with standard approaches for online linear regression. Additionally, we prove that meta-learning inherently incurs a worst-case exponential dependence on the representation dimension, and that this dependence is necessary. Consequently, our upper and lower bounds fully characterize the sample complexity of meta-learning in online linear regression. We also present a general framework for meta-learning that unifies existing techniques and offers a pathway for future advancements. Our framework is both computationally efficient and provably near-optimal. In contrast to recent meta-learning methods, our approach is the first to offer a rigorous theoretical guarantee. Finally, we apply our method to the problem of domain adaptation in matrix completion. Our results demonstrate that meta-learning can substantially reduce the sample complexity required to solve matrix completion in a new domain, particularly when domains share similar structures. We further prove that our sample complexity bounds are tight. Our findings suggest that meta-learning can be effectively leveraged to minimize data requirements in specific applications. Moreover, we prove that meta-learning can achieve optimal sample complexity in the worst case only under the assumption that domain structures are similar. This highlights the critical role of structural similarity in meta-learning. While Massively Multilingual Models (MMMs) have significantly transformed machine translation, their deployment in production environments often encounters practical hurdles. Consequently, recent research has focused on adapting these models to function as lightweight systems suitable for specific low-resource markets through approaches like quantization and distillation. This study evaluates the efficacy of these methods by introducing a new stability metric designed to assess how robustly market characteristics persist during adaptation. Our findings indicate that distillation offers greater stability than quantization, particularly in very low-resource scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate that combining distillation with quantization yields the highest stability, achieving a superior balance between performance and stability that surpasses either approach used in isolation. This robustness suggests that such methods are better equipped to generalize across multiple markets simultaneously. Finally, we propose a unified framework for adaptation that integrates various techniques, including quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation, to facilitate their joint analysis. Extensive experiments confirm that this framework produces models with enhanced stability and generalization capabilities. The accompanying code and experiments are accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/models_stability. Our results underscore the necessity of rigorously assessing model stability during multilingual adaptation, particularly when targeting specific low-resource markets. By prioritizing stability, we aim to mitigate the risk of overfitting to individual markets and inadvertently introducing biases. Ultimately, this work seeks to advance the field of mass-language modeling by fostering the creation of more robust, generalizable, and fair multilingual systems. The paper concludes with a discussion on the broader implications of our research and outlines potential future directions. This work was conducted while the authors were affiliated with Google. Controllable image captioning involves generating diverse descriptions for the same image based on specific user inputs, such as questions or prompts. While current methods typically depend on pre-trained models with fixed architectures, this paper introduces a flexible, prompt-based system that allows for fine-grained control over various caption types through novel prompts. We present CAPTIONS, a proposed framework that adapts a single base answer-generator by separating the focus on question understanding from caption generation. This design enables a single system to produce multiple distinct caption responses. Additionally, we define four categories of captions based on user queries and train the framework using questions collected from social media. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms previous methods in producing diverse and accurate responses. Finally, we explore potential applications of this theoretical structure in legal contexts. Speech translation involves converting spoken audio from one language into written text in another. Although neural machine translation (NMT) has surpassed statistical methods, significant performance gains are now increasingly difficult to achieve. Zero-shot speech translation (ZSST) offers a solution by eliminating the need for parallel data in the target language. This paper introduces a ZSST framework utilizing a large-scale multilingual end-to-end model trained solely on parallel spoken data across all source and target language pairs. To effectively manage the vast number of language pairs, we implement a semi-supervised training strategy that leverages both large-scale multilingual attention-based encoder-decoder architectures and character-level neural machine translation techniques. Our model is evaluated on the ZSST benchmark within the 2020 Interspeech ZSST evaluation task. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive performance compared to the ZSST baseline, while also outperforming recent limited-resource ZSST methods. We introduce a novel formulation and extension of classical heat conduction theory, encompassing cases with or without fading memory, which subsumes the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions as a specific instance. This study examines the well-posedness of systems featuring dynamic boundary conditions on the right-hand side, incorporating a broad class of fading memory-type terms on the left-hand side. These equations generalize the classical Coleman-Gurtin model with dynamic boundary conditions to domains possessing memory properties. Furthermore, the classical Newton cooling condition emerges as a specific case. For boundary domains exhibiting memory, we demonstrate that the temperature system can be decoupled into a thermal equation in the bulk coupled with non-isothermal phase-field equations on the boundary, alongside a finite-dimensional dynamical system representing the energy balance. These representations offer an alternative perspective for analyzing long-term behavior. Additionally, we establish exponential stability for these representations within the uniform case. Finally, we outline an extension to non-uniform situations and provide a sketch of the asymptotic behavior for a simplified model where internal fading memory is absent. In this specific scenario, we show that the uniform system constitutes a global attractor for the general system within an appropriate topology. This result serves as a foundational step toward proving analogous outcomes for the general system equipped with internal fading memory. The proofs rely on energy estimates, spectral gap inequalities, and various technical lemmas. The methodology is robust and applicable to other systems involving Coleman-Gurtin type equations with memory. This work serves as a preliminary step toward achieving such results when internal fading memory is present. The current analysis draws upon the author's thesis, with some aspects developed in collaboration with other researchers. Specifically, the boundary integral term in the energy inequality was derived in [1], while the spectral gap inequality was established in [2]. The extension to non-uniform scenarios was addressed in [3]. The investigation into long-term behavior is based on the author's thesis [4], alongside [5], where the author contributed to the development of the uniform and non-uniform representations and the proof of the spectral gap inequality. Precise localization and identification of vertebrae are critical for numerous clinical tasks, including vertebra labeling, surgical guidance, and spine deformity assessment. Spinal deformities, such as scoliosis, are prevalent and can severely restrict daily activities. Spine deformity assessment relies on semi-automated methods that require robust localization and identification capabilities. Although deep learning-based approaches have recently been introduced for localization and identification, they often depend on annotated vertebra bounding boxes during training, which are labor-intensive and costly. Furthermore, the complex curvature of the spine in CT images can cause localization techniques to fail. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel method comprising two main components: an unsupervised spine rectification technique and a conic optimization-based identification approach. Our results demonstrate that spines are effectively aligned with a single straight line, and vertebra identification achieves high accuracy with superior robustness. Significantly, our identification method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques while eliminating the need for bounding box annotations. Additionally, the method exhibits resistance to local minima during optimization. We validate our approach using a public CT dataset, achieving an identification accuracy of 89.5% and a deflection error of 0.51. This study investigates the potential of physics-informed machine learning to enhance quadruped locomotion within model-based reinforcement learning frameworks. By utilizing an elastic actuator model and incorporating prior knowledge of the system's dynamics, we demonstrate that integrating this background into the training process yields superior policies compared to non-informed approaches. Furthermore, our results indicate that integrating even minimal physical insights can significantly improve performance, suggesting that this strategy is a viable and effective pathway for developing high-performance robotic controllers. We introduce a quantum variational approach designed to identify whether a given state is mixed. Our primary finding is that this problem can be formulated as minimizing a specific cost function within a quantum variational algorithm. The ground state of the corresponding variational problem signals the separability of the state, while the optimal classical solution provides the measure of nonlocality for a given input. We successfully implemented this algorithm on classical hardware using a near-term quantum circuit and evaluated its performance on the Bell state, maximally mixed state, and GHZ state. Additionally, we conducted an extensive analysis of computational complexity and introduced an update rule for the variational parameters. This algorithm offers a fresh perspective on characterizing multipartite entanglement and nonlocality, with potential applications in quantum key distribution and quantum metrology. Furthermore, it is well-suited for implementation on noisier hardware, including near-term quantum devices. Finally, we outline an extension of this algorithm capable of calculating various entanglement measures. Together, these findings pave the way for developing quantum machine learning algorithms to address fundamental challenges in quantum information theory. Non-Riemannian gravitational frameworks offer significant value for investigating quantum gravity scenarios characterized by preferred frames of reference. The proliferation of wireless devices in homes has rendered IEEE 802.11 the primary communication standard. However, the increasing density of these devices places significant strain on Access Points (APs), often leading to severe performance degradation. This paper introduces a novel scheme leveraging IEEE 802.11k and IEEE 802.11v standards to enable each station to identify the optimal AP or Extender based on the target channel load. This approach facilitates seamless handovers and allows devices to select the best connection point dynamically. The proposed method was validated through both theoretical analysis and extensive simulations using the NS-3 network simulator. Results demonstrate that the scheme significantly outperforms existing IEEE 802.11k/v-based solutions, thereby enhancing overall Home WiFi network performance. Furthermore, the study confirms the model's efficacy in real-world deployments, highlighting its potential to improve connectivity for both current and future 5G applications. Finally, the paper outlines the advantages of the proposed approach and identifies key research challenges for future development.
